docs.text: Driver TMP117 Driver ¶ A C++20 driver for the Texas Instruments TMP117 digital temperature sensor. It waits for the power-up load, checks the Device_ID, runs continuous or one-shot conversions, latches the alert flags and programs the alert limits, on any MCU. Quickstart API guide Source on GitHub The TMP117 is a digital temperature sensor with a 16-bit result in steps of 1/128 °C, accurate to 0.1 °C from -20 °C to 50 °C, a programmable alert window and a small EEPROM, read over I2C or SMBus (1 Features, p. 1 ). TMP117 Figure description and sources The TMP117 in the middle, drawn as its WSON-6 package. On the left the MCU that runs the driver, joined to it by I2C. To the right, what the chip drives, in the order the power flows. Below it, what the chip reads back. The tiles at the bottom are the headline numbers, each with the datasheet section and page it comes from. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . What it does ¶ What the TMP117 does Figure description and sources Each card is one function of the TMP117: an icon, its name and what it does for the application. The filled pill says how this driver covers it (legend below); the outlined pills are the chip registers behind it. The coverage table in the README gives the driver calls and the datasheet section of each card. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . Where it is used ¶ Electronic thermometers Wireless environmental sensors Thermostats Cold chain asset tracking Temperature transmitters Uses named by the datasheet (1 Features, p. 1 ). Inside the sensor ¶ Inside the TMP117 Figure description and sources The TMP117's function blocks inside its outline. Arrows between blocks carry signals or data in the direction they point (both ways where they have two heads). The package pins stand on the left and right edges with their numbers, each wired to the block it reaches. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . Pins and wiring ¶ TMP117 pinout, WSON-6 Figure description and sources The TMP117 seen from the top, in its WSON-6 package. Pin 1 is marked by the dot; the numbers run counter-clockwise from it. Each pad is coloured by the pin's electrical type (legend below). Next to it is the pin's name and, in mono, the hook of the driver's port that drives or reads it; a pin without a hook is not used by the driver. The dashed square is the exposed pad. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . Wiring: Typical connections Figure description and sources The MCU on the left, the TMP117 in the middle. Each wire to the chip is coloured by the chip pin's electrical type and carries the net name and the chip pin number above it and, under it, the driver hooks that use it (and any part on the net). The boxes underneath list the supplies, the support parts and the pins this circuit leaves unconnected. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . TMP117 package, WSON-6 Figure description and sources The TMP117 package seen from the top and, when the height is known, from the side, drawn to scale: 2.0 x 2.0 x 0.8 mm. The arrows carry the datasheet's dimensions, the dot marks pin 1 and the pads are numbered counter-clockwise from it, coloured by the pin's electrical type (legend below). Pads sit centred on each side at the stated pitch; the datasheet's land pattern is the reference for a board. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . TMP117: I2C register word Figure description and sources One I2C register word of the TMP117, 24 bits in a row from the most significant (left, sent first) to the least significant (right). Each row is one kind of frame; each coloured box a field, with its first and last bit number under it. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . High-accuracy digital temperature sensor TMP117 Texas Instruments Function Temperature, 16-bit result at 1/128 °C per count; ±0.1 °C from -20 °C to 50 °C Interface I2C and SMBus, 5 kHz to 400 kHz (the datasheet lists 1 kHz, see A15); 7-bit address 0x48 to 0x4B from the ADD0 pin; one pointer byte, 16-bit words Conversions Continuous (cycle 15.5 ms to 16 s), shutdown, or one-shot; averaging of 1, 8, 32 or 64 conversions Alert High and low limits on an open-drain ALERT pin: alert mode or therm mode, either polarity, or data-ready Memory EEPROM for the power-on configuration, limits and offset, one user word and two traceability words Supply 1.8 V to 5.5 V (1.7 V up to 70 °C); 3.5 µA at one result per second, 0.15 µA in shutdown Every pin, the reference circuits, the bus settings, the timing and the power: Hardware . Quick start ¶ Wire the chip as above, write the port for your MCU ( Porting ), then: #include "tmp117.hpp" int read_board_temperature ( MyPort & port , int32_t & milli_celsius ) { tmp117 :: TMP117 < MyPort > sensor ( port ); // address 0x48 (ADD0 to GND), no I/O yet if ( auto r = sensor . EnsureInitialized (); ! r ) { // 1. wait for the power-up load, Device_ID, config return static_cast < int > ( r . error ); // Bus, Timeout or DeviceIdMismatch: wiring } const auto t = sensor . ReadTemperatureMilliC (); // 2. the latest continuous result if ( ! t ) { return static_cast < int > ( t . error ); // NoMeasurement: wait one cycle and ask again } milli_celsius = t . value ; // 3. thousandths of a degree Celsius, 7.8125 mC per count return 0 ; } Every step, with the port and what to check when it does not work: Quickstart . Driver coverage ¶ Capability What the chip does Driver API Registers Status Datasheet Temperature A 16-bit result, 7.8125 m°C per count, never the 8000h value before a conversion ReadTemperatureRaw , ReadTemperatureMilliC Temp_Result ( kTempResult ) Supported 7.3.3, p. 13 Averaging and cycle time 1, 8, 32 or 64 conversions per result and eight cycle times, checked against Table 7-7 SetAveraging , SetCycleTime Configuration ( kConfiguration ) Supported 7.6.3, p. 27 Continuous, shutdown, one-shot Converts continuously, sleeps at 0.15 µA, or takes one result on request SetMode , StartOneShot , ReadOneShotMilliC , WaitDataReady Configuration ( kConfiguration ) Supported 7.4, p. 14 Alert window and therm ALERT outside a window (alert mode) or above a limit with hysteresis (therm mode), flags latched SetAlertFunction , SetAlertPolarity , SetAlertSource , SetLimits , ReadStatus , ReadAlertPin THigh_Limit ( kHighLimit ), TLow_Limit ( kLowLimit ) Supported 7.4.4, p. 15 Offset trim The chip adds a signed offset to every result, up to ±256 °C in 7.8125 m°C steps SetOffsetMilliC Temp_Offset ( kTempOffset ) Supported 7.6.9, p. 31 Power-on defaults Stores the configuration, limits and offset so the chip starts alone; every step checked and relocked ProgramPowerOnDefaults , ProgramUserWord EEPROM_UL ( kEepromUnlock ), EEPROM2 ( kEeprom2 ) Guarded 7.5.1, p. 18 Identity and traceability Checks Device_ID before anything else and reads the two NIST traceability words EnsureInitialized , ReadUniqueId , GetRevision Device_ID ( kDeviceId ), EEPROM1 ( kEeprom1 ), EEPROM3 ( kEeprom3 ) Supported 7.6.11, p. 32 Soft and general-call reset Soft reset by default; the bus-wide general-call reset only when you opt in SoftReset , GeneralCallReset Configuration ( kConfiguration ) Guarded 7.6.3, p. 27 SMBus alert response The bus-wide alert address read; the driver returns Unsupported and says why - - Not covered 7.5.3.1, p. 20 Supported : the driver covers it and a host test checks it; Guarded : covered, behind an explicit acknowledgement because a wrong value can do harm; Not covered : the chip has it and the driver leaves it alone. From docs/hardware.yml ; kokeb-docs hardware --check confirms that every API name is in inc/tmp117.hpp and every register (the header constant in brackets, where the header spells it otherwise) in inc/tmp117_registers.hpp . The driver has no platform code. You give it a small class that brings the bus up and moves bytes; it does the rest: the power-up wait, the Device_ID check, register framing, unit conversion, the flag latch and every timeout. What you get ¶ One object per chip. TMP117<YourPort> takes a reference to your port and does no I/O until EnsureInitialized() . See API guide . Errors you can act on. Every call returns Result<T> with an Error such as Bus , Timeout , DeviceIdMismatch , NoMeasurement or UnexpectedReset . See API guide . Datasheet defaults. Config{} holds the chip's reset values, with units in the field names. See Configuration . A guarded EEPROM path. One call programs the power-on defaults, relocks the chip on every failure path and verifies the result. See API guide . The open questions in the open. Each place the datasheet is silent or contradicts itself is listed with the driver's choice and the switch that tests the other reading. See Ambiguities . Zero-overhead portability. The port is a CRTP class checked by a concept: the bus hooks and a delay, plus an optional ALERT-pin hook and logging found at compile time. See Porting . No heap, no exceptions, no RTTI. The host tests build with -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti . See Contract . Tested without hardware. Host tests run the driver against a register model of the chip written from the datasheet alone. See Testing and CI . Datasheet ¶ Document Revision Get it Datasheet: TMP117 High-Accuracy, Low-Power, Digital Temperature Sensor With SMBus- and I2C-Compatible Interface (Texas Instruments SNOSD82D) D, September 2022 PDF · vendor page Application note: Precise Temperature Measurements With TMP116 and TMP117 (Texas Instruments SNOA986) A, 2019-08 PDF · vendor page Application note: Fixed-point interpretation of the temperature output (Texas Instruments SBAA588) A, 2025-01 PDF · vendor page Application note: Alert and therm threshold design across temperature sensors (Texas Instruments SDAA311) none stated, 2026-03 PDF · vendor page Written against these revisions; the SHA-256 of each file is in docs/datasheets.yml . Where each part of the driver is in the datasheet: Datasheet map . Where to go next ¶ Quickstart Wire the chip, write the port, read a temperature in about 15 lines. Hardware Pins, bus settings, timing and power. Contract What the driver promises, what it needs, threading and errors. API guide Initialise, configure, measure and handle errors, task by task. Porting Implement the port for your MCU. API reference Every class and member, generated from the headers.

docs.text: Agent context ¶ What an agent needs before it touches this repository: the flow, the skill for each step, the exact local checks, the file layout, the standing rules, the pitfalls that failed CI before, and when to stop. Read AGENTS.md for the repository itself. This page is managed by the template ( scaffold.py --check-drift --fix ships it) and tools/check_skills.py checks that every skill named here exists and that the files its commands name exist. 1. The flow and the skill for each step ¶ Each step has an input, an output and an exit rule. Do not skip a step and do not start the next before the exit rule holds. # Step Skill Output Exit rule 0 Plan: new driver, extension or duplicate, and the API shape plan-driver placement.md with a verdict Verdict NEW ; otherwise stop or extend 1 Scaffold new-driver-from-template A building driver with the example chip renamed verify passes on the untouched scaffold 2 Build from the datasheet datasheet-conformance , add-driver-feature , add-port Register map, model, tests, driver, port, examples, docs Host tests green; every datasheet topic recorded 3 Self-review cpp20-profile , misra-review , hardware-lessons-review Findings fixed Every catalogue class in recurring-defects.md answered 4 Verify verify Local gate result tools/preflight.sh ends 0 failure(s) 5 Independent review review-round A report per round NO BLOCKER and no MAJOR 6 First-push gate first-push Container rehearsal and the evidence list 0 failure(s) and 0 gate failure(s) 7 Publish publish-driver Public repository, one commit, green main , Pages CI gate / gate green on main ; the owner did the owner-only steps 8 Release candidate release Tag v0.1.0-rc.N Release workflow green; checksums verified 9 Hardware hardware-validation Level H0, H1 or H2 stated and evidenced Badge, driver.yml and release text agree 10 After release bump-pin A pin-bump pull request per consumer Consumer CI green A change to an existing driver skips steps 0, 1 and 7: use add-driver-feature or add-port , then steps 3 to 5 and a pull request (AGENTS.md, "Branches, commits and pull requests"). The agent safety-reviewer runs the review skills read-only. 2. The local gate: commands and what passes ¶ Run from the repository root. Set VENV (a venv with the docs theme, lizard, yamllint), CI_TOOLS_DIR (a kokeb-labs/ci-tools checkout) and CLANG_TIDY (version 20) when the tools are not on PATH . A step the preflight skips is named in its last line: install the tool; do not push around it. Command Passes when tools/preflight.sh Last line == 0 failure(s) and no skip you can fix tools/preflight.sh --container 0 failure(s) and 0 gate failure(s) (coverage, ASan/UBSan, fuzz in the CI image) python3 tools/scaffold.py --check-drift . no template drift (or each difference is listed under local with a reason) python3 tools/check_standalone.py Exit 0: no other project's name, no dated history, the right copyright holder python3 -I tools/check_skills.py Every skill named in this page exists, has front matter, and names existing files python3 -I tools/check_layout.py One source per header, SDK code only in src/boundary/ python3 -I tools/check_hardware.py driver.yml hardware level, README badge and rig document agree python3 -I tools/check_language.py driver.yml language: block and every place that repeats the C++ standard agree ( --fix rewrites them) python3 tools/misra_lint.py --root . No error; fix warnings in files you touch kokeb-docs figures && kokeb-docs gen && kokeb-docs check No diff afterwards ( git diff --exit-code docs README.md ) mkdocs build -f _config/mkdocs.yml --strict -d /tmp/site Exit 0, no warning git ls-files | grep -i '\.pdf$' No output git add -A && git ls-files -s examples/esp32/scripts Mode 160000 (a gitlink), if examples/esp32 exists CI-only checks, which a workstation cannot run: the MISRA scan and the ESP32 builds. Cover them by reading the misra-review skill and building examples/esp32 with the ESP-IDF version in examples/esp32/app_config.yml (the scripts are in examples/esp32/scripts , Platforms ) when ESP-IDF is installed. Delete the build directories afterwards; never run docker system prune or any other prune on a shared machine. Run one container job at a time and cmake --build ... --parallel 3 at most when other agents are working. 3. File layout ¶ One source per header, same stem. inc/<stem>.hpp has src/<stem>.cpp (or .ipp for a header-only template driver). A header that declares only constants, types, details, registers, the Kconfig defaults or the port contract ( _types , _detail , _registers , _kconfig , _interface ) needs no source. A header with real logic always has its own source. A header that holds only templates, constants or inline types may instead be listed under header_only in tools/layout.yml with a one-line reason (no colon followed by a space in it); nothing else is exempt. No combined file ( a_and_b.cpp ): split it by header. SDK-touching code (ESP-IDF, an RTOS, a vendor HAL) is never in inc/ or in src/ 's logic: it lives one file per SDK component in src/boundary/<component>.cpp , named after the component, so the directory carries the layering rule. A driver normally has none: it reaches hardware only through the port hooks, and the SDK appears only in examples/<platform>/ . The only generated SDK header read by the driver is sdkconfig.h , in inc/<name>_kconfig.hpp . examples/<platform>/ is the only platform code; examples/host/ always exists. Tests do not include SDK headers. Tool configuration is in _config/ only: no copies or symlinks at the root. The root holds only the files AGENTS.md lists. Never commit build*/ , a venv, a PDF, logs or a scratch file. tools/layout.yml (optional) lists the exceptions: header_only , internal , boundary_extra , each with a reason that tools/check_layout.py also keeps current. 4. Naming ¶ Namespace and package are the part number in lower case; files <name>.hpp , <name>_<topic>.hpp ; public methods PascalCase, private camelBack, members snake_case_ , constants kPascalCase , units as suffixes ( TimeoutMs , VoltageMv ); include guards <NAME>_<FILE_STEM>_<EXT> ; enumerations enum class with EnumLast , never a sentinel value; chip-specific Error values from 16. The repository is driver-<part> ; the copyright holder is The driver-<part> authors . Full rules: AGENTS.md and the handbook. 5. Docs and diagrams ¶ Every claim about the chip cites a datasheet section and page; docs/datasheets.yml records vendor, number, revision, date, URL, SHA-256 and one topic per section used. The PDF itself is never committed. docs/hardware.yml is the one description of the chip (package, pins, supply, hooks, blocks, a circuit, the README's overview, capabilities and frames). The pinout, outline, block diagram, wiring and frame figures, the chip card and the coverage table are generated from it and the headers: never draw or type them by hand. The README and docs/index.md lead with the chip (summary, hero figure, capabilities, uses, inside the chip, pins and wiring), then the quick start and the driver coverage; the layering figure is on the architecture page only. docs/bus.md shows the bus: a timing figure per bus the driver uses ( docs/model/<name>.timing.yml : the waveform and a param with ref for every time and rate) and a topology figure when the datasheet describes a daisy chain or several devices on one bus ( docs/model/<name>.topology.yml ). A number without a datasheet reference fails kokeb-docs figures ; fill in data, never draw. Code shown on the site lives in tests/docs/ between --8<-- markers and is compiled. Every public symbol has a Doxygen comment. CHANGELOG.md has ## [Unreleased] with the allowed headings only. A claim of behaviour in docs, comments or the build report names the code and the test that back it (RD-09). Anything only a bench can confirm is marked not verified on hardware with bench steps, and the level is stated ( hardware-validation skill). 6. Standing rules ¶ Stand-alone. The repository describes its own part and nothing else: no product, board, project, person or other repository by name, no lab history, no dates outside release headings, datasheet revisions and waiver expiries. Behaviour learned on a bench is written as the design with its datasheet section. Copyright is The <repo> authors in LICENSE , every source header, driver.yml and the docs footer. Do not put a company or a person there. No attribution. No Co-Authored-By: trailers, "Generated with" footers or tool names in commits, pull requests or files. Commits are signed off ( git commit -s ) with the owner's GitHub noreply address; no personal email address appears anywhere, and security reports go through GitHub advisories ( .github/SECURITY.md ). No secrets (tokens, keys, credentials, personal addresses) and no vendor PDFs or other licensed documents anywhere in the tree, the history, a pull request or a log you attach. Datasheets are fetched only from the vendor's public page into a scratch folder; never bypass a login or a 403, never fetch the same blocked URL again; record the gap and stop that item. Owner-only actions: making a repository public, rulesets and security settings, deleting or recreating a repository, force-pushing, the final release tag. publish-driver lists them. Ask; do not assume. No force-push to main and no history rewrite of a published branch. Never move or delete a tag. docs.text: Each step has an input, an output and an exit rule. Do not skip a step and do not start the next before the exit rule holds. # Step Skill Output Exit rule 0 Plan: new driver, extension or duplicate, and the API shape plan-driver placement.md with a verdict Verdict NEW ; otherwise stop or extend 1 Scaffold new-driver-from-template A building driver with the example chip renamed verify passes on the untouched scaffold 2 Build from the datasheet datasheet-conformance , add-driver-feature , add-port Register map, model, tests, driver, port, examples, docs Host tests green; every datasheet topic recorded 3 Self-review cpp20-profile , misra-review , hardware-lessons-review Findings fixed Every catalogue class in recurring-defects.md answered 4 Verify verify Local gate result tools/preflight.sh ends 0 failure(s) 5 Independent review review-round A report per round NO BLOCKER and no MAJOR 6 First-push gate first-push Container rehearsal and the evidence list 0 failure(s) and 0 gate failure(s) 7 Publish publish-driver Public repository, one commit, green main , Pages CI gate / gate green on main ; the owner did the owner-only steps 8 Release candidate release Tag v0.1.0-rc.N Release workflow green; checksums verified 9 Hardware hardware-validation Level H0, H1 or H2 stated and evidenced Badge, driver.yml and release text agree 10 After release bump-pin A pin-bump pull request per consumer Consumer CI green A change to an existing driver skips steps 0, 1 and 7: use add-driver-feature or add-port , then steps 3 to 5 and a pull request (AGENTS.md, "Branches, commits and pull requests"). docs.title: 2. The local gate: commands and what passes

docs.text: One source per header, same stem. inc/<stem>.hpp has src/<stem>.cpp (or .ipp for a header-only template driver). A header that declares only constants, types, details, registers, the Kconfig defaults or the port contract ( _types , _detail , _registers , _kconfig , _interface ) needs no source. A header with real logic always has its own source. A header that holds only templates, constants or inline types may instead be listed under header_only in tools/layout.yml with a one-line reason (no colon followed by a space in it); nothing else is exempt. No combined file ( a_and_b.cpp ): split it by header. SDK-touching code (ESP-IDF, an RTOS, a vendor HAL) is never in inc/ or in src/ 's logic: it lives one file per SDK component in src/boundary/<component>.cpp , named after the component, so the directory carries the layering rule. A driver normally has none: it reaches hardware only through the port hooks, and the SDK appears only in examples/<platform>/ . The only generated SDK header read by the driver is sdkconfig.h , in inc/<name>_kconfig.hpp . examples/<platform>/ is the only platform code; examples/host/ always exists. Tests do not include SDK headers. Tool configuration is in _config/ only: no copies or symlinks at the root. The root holds only the files AGENTS.md lists. Never commit build*/ , a venv, a PDF, logs or a scratch file. tools/layout.yml (optional) lists the exceptions: header_only , internal , boundary_extra , each with a reason that tools/check_layout.py also keeps current.
docs.title: 3. File layout

docs.text: Namespace and package are the part number in lower case; files <name>.hpp , <name>_<topic>.hpp ; public methods PascalCase, private camelBack, members snake_case_ , constants kPascalCase , units as suffixes ( TimeoutMs , VoltageMv ); include guards <NAME>_<FILE_STEM>_<EXT> ; enumerations enum class with EnumLast , never a sentinel value; chip-specific Error values from 16. The repository is driver-<part> ; the copyright holder is The driver-<part> authors . Full rules: AGENTS.md and the handbook.
docs.title: 4. Naming

docs.text: Every claim about the chip cites a datasheet section and page; docs/datasheets.yml records vendor, number, revision, date, URL, SHA-256 and one topic per section used. The PDF itself is never committed. docs/hardware.yml is the one description of the chip (package, pins, supply, hooks, blocks, a circuit, the README's overview, capabilities and frames). The pinout, outline, block diagram, wiring and frame figures, the chip card and the coverage table are generated from it and the headers: never draw or type them by hand. The README and docs/index.md lead with the chip (summary, hero figure, capabilities, uses, inside the chip, pins and wiring), then the quick start and the driver coverage; the layering figure is on the architecture page only. docs/bus.md shows the bus: a timing figure per bus the driver uses ( docs/model/<name>.timing.yml : the waveform and a param with ref for every time and rate) and a topology figure when the datasheet describes a daisy chain or several devices on one bus ( docs/model/<name>.topology.yml ). A number without a datasheet reference fails kokeb-docs figures ; fill in data, never draw. Code shown on the site lives in tests/docs/ between --8<-- markers and is compiled. Every public symbol has a Doxygen comment. CHANGELOG.md has ## [Unreleased] with the allowed headings only. A claim of behaviour in docs, comments or the build report names the code and the test that back it (RD-09). Anything only a bench can confirm is marked not verified on hardware with bench steps, and the level is stated ( hardware-validation skill).

docs.text: Stand-alone. The repository describes its own part and nothing else: no product, board, project, person or other repository by name, no lab history, no dates outside release headings, datasheet revisions and waiver expiries. Behaviour learned on a bench is written as the design with its datasheet section. Copyright is The <repo> authors in LICENSE , every source header, driver.yml and the docs footer. Do not put a company or a person there. No attribution. No Co-Authored-By: trailers, "Generated with" footers or tool names in commits, pull requests or files. Commits are signed off ( git commit -s ) with the owner's GitHub noreply address; no personal email address appears anywhere, and security reports go through GitHub advisories ( .github/SECURITY.md ). docs.text: Ambiguities ¶ Where the datasheet is silent, says two things, or gives only a typical value, and what the driver does about it. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Texas Instruments SNOSD82D D: Power-up, the EEPROM load and the first result: 7.3.1 Power-Up, p. 12 EEPROM, unlock and programming: 7.5.1 EEPROM Overview, p. 18 SMBus alert response and general call: 7.5.3.1.5 SMBus Alert Function; 7.5.3.1.6 General-Call Reset Function, p. 22 Limit registers and the offset register: 7.6.4 THigh_Limit; 7.6.5 TLow_Limit (p. 29); 7.6.9 Temperature Offset (p. 31), p. 29 Device ID and the revision field: 7.6.11 Device ID Register, p. 32 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . Every row is a reading of SNOSD82D (Rev. D) that could be wrong. The driver picks the reading that is safe when the other one is true, and the host model has a switch for each reading, so the whole safety test suite runs under both ( tests/test_faults.cpp , tests/test_eeprom.cpp ). Nothing here was measured on a chip: the driver is at hardware level H0, so a bench run is what turns a reading into a fact. Decisions taken for the first release ¶ These four questions had more than one reasonable answer; the owner's defaults are recorded here with the knob that changes them. Q1: how the chip is locked again after programming ¶ The datasheet describes the EEPROM unlock bit (EUN) and says the general-call reset or a power cycle clears it. A general-call reset resets every device on the bus that answers the general call, not only this chip. The driver therefore locks with a soft reset by default , after writing EUN = 0 and reading it back, and it sends the general-call reset only when the caller sets Config::allow_general_call . If the lock cannot be confirmed and the opt-in is off, the call returns EepromVerifyFailed and tells you to power-cycle the chip. The soft-reset word is never written into the EEPROM. Knob: Config::allow_general_call (driver), eun_write_zero_locks , soft_reset_clears_eun (model). Q2: limits in the wrong order ¶ SetLimits() and Validate() refuse a low limit above the high limit . See A10 . Q3: SMBus alert response ¶ The SMBus alert response is a read of the bus-wide address 0x0C , in which every alerting device answers and the lowest address wins. It cannot be done safely through a port that models one device, and the chip's ALERT pin plus ReadStatus() already tell the host which chip alerts. SmbusAlertResponse() returns Unsupported and sends nothing in this release. Knob: none; the model counts ara_reads to prove nothing is sent. Q4: the two waits ¶ The datasheet gives the power-up load (1.5 ms) and one EEPROM word (about 7 ms) as typical values only. The driver waits the typical time and then polls EEPROM_Busy up to a deadline of 10 ms and 50 ms : see A1 and A2 . The switch-off of a driver that lost track of the chip does not poll: it has its own budget of two 7 ms waits and returns Timeout with nothing sent when the chip is still busy. What the datasheet leaves open ¶ Id The question What the driver does Model knob A1 The power-up load takes 1.5 ms typical, no maximum Wait 1.5 ms, then poll EEPROM_Busy, deadline reset_timeout_ms (10 ms) por_load_us A2 One EEPROM word takes about 7 ms typical, no maximum Wait 7 ms, then poll, deadline eeprom_timeout_ms (50 ms) eeprom_program_us A3 EEPROM2 reads 0000h in one place and an unknown value in another Never assume its value eeprom2_reset A4 Whether Temp_Offset is a stored power-on value Program it only when asked, as a power-on value, and read it back offset_in_eeprom A5 Whether a soft reset reloads the EEPROM and clears EUN Lock with EUN = 0, then reset, then confirm by reading EUN soft_reset_clears_eun , soft_reset_reloads A6 Whether writing EUN = 0 locks without a reset Always write EUN = 0 first, then confirm eun_write_zero_locks A7 A saturated minimum could equal the 8000h no-conversion value 8000h is never a temperature saturate_min_8001 A8 Whether "exceeds" means above or at the limit Documented as strict; the tests pass under both limit_compare_inclusive A9 There is no power-on flag Evidence from the setting bits, EEPROM_Busy and 8000h; CheckHealth() none (a blind case, tested) A10 Low above high in therm mode is not described Refused everywhere none (policy) A11 Whether a one-shot sets the alert flag by comparison or always Treated as by comparison oneshot_sets_alert A12 Whether a Configuration read in therm mode clears Data_Ready Latch Data_Ready on every read therm_read_clears_dr A13 The Rev field has no defined values Accept any, report it device_rev A14 A write during the load is "ignored": ACK or NACK Never write after a reply that shows the load; a reset no read has shown is a residual risk por_write_nack A15 Bus timeout is 35 ms typical and 20 to 40 ms in the table Port contract: transactions far below 20 ms none (port) A16 The cycle time has no stated accuracy A one-shot waits one conversion longer than needed osc_error_pct A17 One text says not to erase EEPROM1, another words it for EEPROM[1] Protect both 05h and 08h none (policy) A18 TMP116 and TMP119 IDs are not in this datasheet Only the TMP117 ID passes, with the A13 consequence device_id A19 What MOD reads after a one-shot, 01 or still 11 A one-shot is complete when Data_Ready is seen or MOD reads 01; both readings work oneshot_mod_reads_back_11 A20 Conversions restart while the last word is programmed when the defaults are continuous Documented; choose shutdown in the defaults none (policy) A21 The chip can be left unlocked by an interrupted programming Read EEPROM_UL at start-up and lock first; start-up writes nothing when the lock cannot be confirmed; switch-off writes the lock, then sends unless the read after the last lock write is clean with EUN = 1 ForceUnlock() , eun_write_zero_locks A22 Whether EEPROM_UL can be written, and EUN read, during the load No write follows a busy EEPROM_UL reply, so the driver does not depend on it none A1 and A2: the two waits ¶ SNOSD82D gives 1.5 ms (typical) for the load of the registers from EEPROM after power-up (6.5, p. 7; 7.3.1, p. 12) and about 7 ms (typical) per EEPROM word (6.6, p. 7), and prints no maximum for either. A fixed wait of the typical time would be wrong on a slow part, so the driver waits that time and then polls EEPROM_Busy (bit 12 of Configuration, bit 14 of EEPROM_UL) until it reads 0, up to reset_timeout_ms (10 ms) or eeprom_timeout_ms (50 ms). Start-up and programming write nothing before EEPROM_Busy has read 0. If the deadline passes the call returns Timeout and the driver stays uninitialised. The switch-off of a driver that lost track of the chip uses neither deadline: after a busy EEPROM_UL reply it waits 7 ms and reads again, twice at most in the call (14 ms), and returns Timeout with nothing sent when the chip is still busy ( decision table , rows W1, W2, U6). The model's por_load_us and eeprom_program_us stretch the times to prove every outcome. If you know the maximum: raise or lower the two Config fields; they are limited to 1 ms to 1000 ms. A3: the user word after a reset ¶ The EEPROM2 register is listed with a reset value of 0000h in its own section and with an unknown value in the register map, and the overview names four general-purpose words while the map has three (7.5.1.1, 7.6.8, Table 7-3). The driver does not use the user word for anything, reads it only in ReadUniqueId() , and writes it only in ProgramUserWord() . eeprom2_reset in the model sets its initial value. A4: is the offset stored in EEPROM ¶ Temp_Offset is listed among the registers that load from EEPROM at power-up (Table 7-3, note 1), but the text counts the user-programmable words differently. ProgramPowerOnDefaults() programs the offset word because the caller passes a Config that has an offset, and it reads the word back after the reset; with offset_in_eeprom = false the model keeps the offset out of EEPROM, and the verification then reports EepromVerifyFailed for a non-zero offset instead of claiming success. A5: what the soft reset does ¶ Table 7-6 describes Soft_Reset (Configuration bit 1) as a 2 ms reset, and the register figure shows it as read-only while the table says write. The datasheet does not say whether the soft reset reloads the EEPROM and clears EUN the way the general-call reset does. The driver relocks with EUN = 0 ( A6 ), resets (soft by default, Q1 ), then reads EUN and refuses to succeed unless it reads 0 . Two consequences are worth knowing: If the soft reset does not reload the EEPROM ( soft_reset_reloads = false ), the verification reads back the registers the driver wrote, not the EEPROM, so the verify step is vacuous: it can pass without the EEPROM holding the values. The only proof is a power cycle and a read of the registers. The tests pin this reading and the docs say so; an application that must be sure powers the chip down once after programming. If the soft reset does not clear EUN ( soft_reset_clears_eun = false ) and writing EUN = 0 does not lock either, the driver falls back to the general-call reset when allow_general_call is set, and otherwise returns EepromVerifyFailed with the chip still unlocked, which is why the error text says to power-cycle it. A6: writing EUN as 0 ¶ The datasheet says the general-call reset or a power cycle clears the unlock bit, and describes EUN as a read/write bit without saying that writing 0 locks. The driver writes 0 anyway (up to three attempts, each after waiting for EEPROM_Busy to clear, up to eeprom_timeout_ms ; after that deadline the lock is written whatever EEPROM_Busy reads, a residual risk of a faulty chip) because a locked chip is the safe state, and confirms by reading EUN. With eun_write_zero_locks = false the model ignores that write and only a reset locks it. A7: the offset at the minimum and 8000h ¶ A result that saturates at the minimum would be 8000h, the same word the chip reports before any conversion (7.6.2, 7.6.9). The driver treats 8000h as "no result" or, after a result was seen, as a reset, and never returns it as a temperature. saturate_min_8001 makes the model saturate at 8001h instead, which the driver reads as -255.99 °C. If your offset can push a real temperature to the lower end, the call returns an error and not a wrong number. A8: at exactly the limit ¶ The text says a result "exceeds" the high limit and is "lower than" the low limit (7.4.4.1, 7.4.4.2). The driver documents the strict reading and its tests pass under both: a result one count beyond the limit is flagged in both, a result exactly at the limit only with limit_compare_inclusive . A system that must act at the limit should set the limit one count (7.8125 m°C) inside it. A9: a reset to identical values ¶ The chip has no power-on flag. If it resets and its EEPROM holds exactly the values the driver wrote, nothing in the registers changes, and the only trace is that the next result reads 8000h until the first conversion finishes. The driver reports UnexpectedReset on any of the three pieces of evidence (setting bits changed, EEPROM_Busy set unexpectedly, 8000h after a result), and CheckHealth() re-reads them on demand, but a reset between two conversions to identical values can pass unseen. The evidence comes from Configuration only: a reset that reloads the driver's Configuration word but other limits or another offset passes too, once the first conversion is done (the alert limit and the calibration offset are then the EEPROM's). If that matters, program the power-on defaults so a reset restores the configuration, and use Verify::Device with periodic CheckHealth() . A10: limits in the wrong order ¶ Therm mode with the low limit above the high limit is not described (7.4.4.2). The driver refuses it with InvalidArgument , sending nothing, in Validate() , SetLimits() , Configure() and ProgramPowerOnDefaults() . The two limits are two register writes, so the driver writes them in the order that never puts the low limit above the high limit, in the chip or in its own copy, if the second write fails. A11: the alert flag after a one-shot ¶ 7.4.3 says the data-ready and alert flags are set at the end of a one-shot without saying whether the alert flag is set by comparison. The driver treats the flags as it does for continuous conversion. oneshot_sets_alert makes the model set the flag unconditionally; the tests show that the driver still returns the temperature and does not act on a flag alone. A12: Data_Ready in therm mode ¶ The text says a read of Configuration in therm mode does not clear the alert bits, and is silent about Data_Ready. The driver latches Data_Ready on every read, so it is not lost either way ( therm_read_clears_dr ). Under the reading that a Configuration read does not clear it, a Data_Ready left by an unread continuous conversion can complete a one-shot at once and ReadOneShotMilliC() returns the previous result: a residual risk (D-4). A13: the revision field ¶ Device_ID bits 15:12 are the revision; the register figure shows them as unknown and the table gives a reset of 0h. No revision value is documented. The driver masks the field, accepts any, and returns it from GetRevision() . The consequence is that a TMP119, whose ID is 0x2117 , reads as revision 2 of a TMP117 and is accepted: the driver cannot tell them apart, and it does not claim to. device_rev varies the field in the model. A TMP116 ( 0x1116 in other projects) fails the check with DeviceIdMismatch . A14: writes during the power-up load ¶ The datasheet says writes during the load are ignored and does not say whether they are acknowledged. Start-up and the resets write nothing until EEPROM_Busy has read 0 (twice in a row where it matters), and the switch-off of a driver that lost track never writes after an EEPROM_UL reply that shows the load (rows W1 and R1, also when a settle found the reset first, row I3), so for every path that holds evidence of the reset the answer does not change what the driver does. por_write_nack makes the model NACK such writes; the row tests run under both readings. One case remains, a residual risk : a reset that no read has shown yet (a chip-only brown-out, another master's general call) within 1.5 ms before an initialised switch-off or a setter. Those send with no read first, so the write is ignored: under the ACK reading the call returns Ok , under the NACK reading Bus . The next call that reads Configuration reports UnexpectedReset . A15: the bus timeout ¶ The text gives 35 ms typical for the bus timeout and the table gives 20 ms to 40 ms (7.5.3.1.7, 6.7). The port contract asks for SCL of at least 5 kHz and transactions far below 20 ms. The datasheet lists 1 kHz as the lowest SCL (6.7, p. 7), but a 3-byte write takes 36 clocks (the address and three bytes, nine each), about 36 ms at 1 kHz, above the 20 ms minimum timeout, so 5 kHz is the floor this driver states. The driver has no code for it. A16: the oscillator accuracy ¶ Table 7-7 gives nominal cycle times with no tolerance. A one-shot therefore waits (n + 1) x 17.5 ms for n averaged conversions: one conversion more than needed. osc_error_pct slows the model's oscillator to show the margin holds up to 10 percent. A17: the two traceability words ¶ The text says the traceability identifier in EEPROM1 and EEPROM3 must not be erased, and one passage words it as "EEPROM[1]". The driver protects 05h and 08h both: RegisterBus::WriteWord refuses them, and the EEPROM sequence compares them before and after. A18: other parts in the family ¶ The IDs of the TMP116 and the TMP119 come from other projects, not from a datasheet on file, so only 0x117 in bits 11:0 passes. The cost is the TMP119 case in A13 . device_id in the model changes the ID. A19: MOD while a one-shot runs ¶ The datasheet says only that the device "goes to the low-power shutdown mode" when the conversion is done (7.4.3, p. 15); what MOD reads afterwards is not stated. Two readings are possible: MOD reads 01 (shutdown) when the conversion has finished, or MOD keeps reading 11 until the next write. The driver works with both: a pending one-shot is complete when Data_Ready has been seen since the start, or MOD reads 01 , and while it is pending MOD 11 and MOD 01 are both accepted (only MOD 00, the power-on mode, is reset evidence). When the conversion ended with MOD still 11, the driver treats 11 as shutdown until its next Configuration write, so a later CheckHealth() or settle does not read it as a reset. WaitDataReady() returns when the pending one-shot has completed by either rule. One window remains open: a one-shot started from continuous mode clears Data_Ready with its pre-read, but a continuous conversion that ends between that read and the MOD = 11 write sets it again. The driver then counts the one-shot complete on that flag, and ReadOneShotMilliC() returns the continuous conversion's result (a real temperature, at most one cycle old). The window is the time between two bus transfers. To avoid it, call SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) before StartOneShot() . Bench step, not hardware-verified: start a one-shot from continuous mode at the end of a conversion and compare the result with the next one. Data_Ready clears on the read that sees it, so the driver remembers it. A raw ReadRegister() of Configuration while a one-shot is pending is allowed and remembered the same way; a raw ReadRegister() of Temp_Result (which also clears Data_Ready) is refused with Busy while the one-shot is pending, because its value is not valid yet and the driver could not see the flag go. The model's oneshot_mod_reads_back_11 selects the second reading; the safety suite runs under both. Bench step, not hardware-verified: read Configuration after a one-shot and record MOD. A20: programming the power-on defaults with continuous mode ¶ ProgramPowerOnDefaults() writes the defaults, including a continuous MOD, into Configuration while EUN is set. The datasheet (7.5.1.2) asks to avoid conversions while the EEPROM is unlocked. Only MOD1 is volatile (Table 7-6, notes 1 and 2, p. 28): MOD0 is stored, which is how a continuous power-on mode is programmed, so with continuous defaults the chip converts from that write on, for the 7 ms of its programming and until the relock reset. The driver writes the Configuration word last to keep that window short. Choose Mode::Shutdown in the defaults to avoid it. A21: start-up and switch-off on an unlocked chip ¶ With EUN = 1 every write to a programmable register is stored in EEPROM (7.5.1.2, p. 18, Table 7-10, p. 30), and EUN is cleared only by a general-call reset or a power cycle (and, by A6 , perhaps by a write of 0). A host that restarts during ProgramPowerOnDefaults() , or a lock that failed and was left to a power cycle, leaves the chip unlocked while the driver starts again with no memory of it. Writing the limits, the offset and the configuration would program them as power-on defaults, and every later setter would program EEPROM again (1000 writes minimum endurance, section 6.6). What the driver does: after Device_ID and before its first register write, EnsureInitialized() reads EEPROM_UL. With EUN = 1 it writes EUN = 0 and reads it back (up to three times, as in the relock). If EUN still reads 1 the call returns EepromVerifyFailed (or the bus error of the failed write) and has written nothing else; the application power-cycles the chip or sends the general-call reset itself. Start-up never writes anything else without a confirmed lock. A lock is confirmed only by a clean read-back with EUN = 0: a reply that breaks bits 13:0 is no lock, at start-up as in the relock after programming, even when its EUN bit reads 0. Switch-off is different, because never switching the chip off is the worse failure (RD-05). Its rules are the switch-off decision table . When the driver is not initialised, Deinitialize() and SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) read EEPROM_UL once. EUN = 0 on a clean reply: the shutdown write is sent. Otherwise (EUN = 1, a failed read, or a reply that breaks bits 13:0) the driver writes EUN = 0 and reads it back, at most twice; the lock write programs no EEPROM. Only the read after the last lock write decides: when it is clean and shows EUN = 1, the lock cannot be cleared and the write would be programmed as a power-on default of "shutdown" (the chip would then need a power cycle anyway), so it is refused with EepromVerifyFailed and nothing is sent. A clean EUN = 1 seen before a later lock write is stale and never refuses; a failed or garbled read is no evidence. A chip that answers neither the first read nor the lock write gets nothing more ( Bus ). The residual risk is stated: if every lock write was lost or did not take and no read-back succeeded, the shutdown word is programmed. No write follows a clean EEPROM_UL reply with EEPROM_Busy set (the power-up load or a word being programmed): the driver waits 7 ms and reads again, twice at most, and returns Timeout with nothing sent when the chip is still busy. The whole call makes at most 8 transfers and waits at most 14 ms. An initialised driver is always locked (it became initialised only after a confirmed lock), so its switch-off needs no extra read, unless its settle finds reset evidence (row I3). Two residual risks are stated in the contract : row U5 above, and one bit flipped on the bus in the first EEPROM_UL reply of an unlocked chip (EUN read as 0 with bits 13:0 clean). The bus has no CRC, so the driver takes that reply for a lock and writes one word: start-up programs one limit as a power-on default and then fails its read-back, switch-off row U1 programs the shutdown word. It needs an interrupted programming and a bus error on exactly that read; the cost is one EEPROM word. Knob: the model's ForceUnlock() leaves EUN set as an interrupted programming does; eun_write_zero_locks = false makes the lock write ineffective. Bench step, not hardware-verified: interrupt a programming and read EEPROM_UL at the next start. A22: EEPROM_UL during the power-up load ¶ 7.5.1.1 names only the limit registers and Configuration as ignored during the load; it says nothing about a write to EEPROM_UL then, or about whether EUN reads valid while EEPROM_Busy is set. The switch-off writes nothing after a busy EEPROM_UL reply and reads again after the wait, so neither answer changes what it does. A lock write after a failed read (no evidence) may still land in a load; it programs nothing either way. Knob: none. Bench step, not hardware-verified: power-cycle the chip and read EEPROM_UL within 1 ms. How the safety tests use these ¶ tests/test_faults.cpp runs a whole session (start, set limits and alert function, read, one-shot, program a user word, deinitialise) under each reading above and checks that the driver never wrote while the chip was loading or busy, never wrote a traceability or read-only register or an undefined pointer, and never left the EEPROM unlocked. That session waits out every load it causes; the switch-off rows W1, I3 and R1 in tests/test_switch_off.cpp switch off inside the load, with no time passing, under both readings of A14. tests/test_eeprom.cpp covers A2, A5 and A6 in both readings and every failure path of the relock; tests/test_safety_regressions.cpp covers A19 and A21 in both readings, and tests/test_switch_off.cpp every row of the switch-off decision table.

docs.text: Where the datasheet is silent, says two things, or gives only a typical value, and what the driver does about it. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Texas Instruments SNOSD82D D: Power-up, the EEPROM load and the first result: 7.3.1 Power-Up, p. 12 EEPROM, unlock and programming: 7.5.1 EEPROM Overview, p. 18 SMBus alert response and general call: 7.5.3.1.5 SMBus Alert Function; 7.5.3.1.6 General-Call Reset Function, p. 22 Limit registers and the offset register: 7.6.4 THigh_Limit; 7.6.5 TLow_Limit (p. 29); 7.6.9 Temperature Offset (p. 31), p. 29 Device ID and the revision field: 7.6.11 Device ID Register, p. 32 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . Every row is a reading of SNOSD82D (Rev. D) that could be wrong. The driver picks the reading that is safe when the other one is true, and the host model has a switch for each reading, so the whole safety test suite runs under both ( tests/test_faults.cpp , tests/test_eeprom.cpp ). Nothing here was measured on a chip: the driver is at hardware level H0, so a bench run is what turns a reading into a fact.

docs.title: Decisions taken for the first release

docs.text: The datasheet describes the EEPROM unlock bit (EUN) and says the general-call reset or a power cycle clears it. A general-call reset resets every device on the bus that answers the general call, not only this chip. The driver therefore locks with a soft reset by default , after writing EUN = 0 and reading it back, and it sends the general-call reset only when the caller sets Config::allow_general_call . If the lock cannot be confirmed and the opt-in is off, the call returns EepromVerifyFailed and tells you to power-cycle the chip. The soft-reset word is never written into the EEPROM. Knob: Config::allow_general_call (driver), eun_write_zero_locks , soft_reset_clears_eun (model).
docs.title: Q1: how the chip is locked again after programming

docs.text: SetLimits() and Validate() refuse a low limit above the high limit . See A10 .
docs.title: Q2: limits in the wrong order

docs.text: The SMBus alert response is a read of the bus-wide address 0x0C , in which every alerting device answers and the lowest address wins. It cannot be done safely through a port that models one device, and the chip's ALERT pin plus ReadStatus() already tell the host which chip alerts. SmbusAlertResponse() returns Unsupported and sends nothing in this release. Knob: none; the model counts ara_reads to prove nothing is sent.
docs.title: Q3: SMBus alert response

docs.text: The datasheet gives the power-up load (1.5 ms) and one EEPROM word (about 7 ms) as typical values only. The driver waits the typical time and then polls EEPROM_Busy up to a deadline of 10 ms and 50 ms : see A1 and A2 . The switch-off of a driver that lost track of the chip does not poll: it has its own budget of two 7 ms waits and returns Timeout with nothing sent when the chip is still busy.

docs.text: SNOSD82D gives 1.5 ms (typical) for the load of the registers from EEPROM after power-up (6.5, p. 7; 7.3.1, p. 12) and about 7 ms (typical) per EEPROM word (6.6, p. 7), and prints no maximum for either. A fixed wait of the typical time would be wrong on a slow part, so the driver waits that time and then polls EEPROM_Busy (bit 12 of Configuration, bit 14 of EEPROM_UL) until it reads 0, up to reset_timeout_ms (10 ms) or eeprom_timeout_ms (50 ms). Start-up and programming write nothing before EEPROM_Busy has read 0. If the deadline passes the call returns Timeout and the driver stays uninitialised. The switch-off of a driver that lost track of the chip uses neither deadline: after a busy EEPROM_UL reply it waits 7 ms and reads again, twice at most in the call (14 ms), and returns Timeout with nothing sent when the chip is still busy ( decision table , rows W1, W2, U6). The model's por_load_us and eeprom_program_us stretch the times to prove every outcome. If you know the maximum: raise or lower the two Config fields; they are limited to 1 ms to 1000 ms.
docs.title: A1 and A2: the two waits

docs.text: The datasheet says only that the device "goes to the low-power shutdown mode" when the conversion is done (7.4.3, p. 15); what MOD reads afterwards is not stated. Two readings are possible: MOD reads 01 (shutdown) when the conversion has finished, or MOD keeps reading 11 until the next write. The driver works with both: a pending one-shot is complete when Data_Ready has been seen since the start, or MOD reads 01 , and while it is pending MOD 11 and MOD 01 are both accepted (only MOD 00, the power-on mode, is reset evidence). When the conversion ended with MOD still 11, the driver treats 11 as shutdown until its next Configuration write, so a later CheckHealth() or settle does not read it as a reset. WaitDataReady() returns when the pending one-shot has completed by either rule. One window remains open: a one-shot started from continuous mode clears Data_Ready with its pre-read, but a continuous conversion that ends between that read and the MOD = 11 write sets it again. The driver then counts the one-shot complete on that flag, and ReadOneShotMilliC() returns the continuous conversion's result (a real temperature, at most one cycle old). The window is the time between two bus transfers. To avoid it, call SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) before StartOneShot() . Bench step, not hardware-verified: start a one-shot from continuous mode at the end of a conversion and compare the result with the next one. Data_Ready clears on the read that sees it, so the driver remembers it. A raw ReadRegister() of Configuration while a one-shot is pending is allowed and remembered the same way; a raw ReadRegister() of Temp_Result (which also clears Data_Ready) is refused with Busy while the one-shot is pending, because its value is not valid yet and the driver could not see the flag go. The model's oneshot_mod_reads_back_11 selects the second reading; the safety suite runs under both. Bench step, not hardware-verified: read Configuration after a one-shot and record MOD.
docs.title: A19: MOD while a one-shot runs

docs.text: ProgramPowerOnDefaults() writes the defaults, including a continuous MOD, into Configuration while EUN is set. The datasheet (7.5.1.2) asks to avoid conversions while the EEPROM is unlocked. Only MOD1 is volatile (Table 7-6, notes 1 and 2, p. 28): MOD0 is stored, which is how a continuous power-on mode is programmed, so with continuous defaults the chip converts from that write on, for the 7 ms of its programming and until the relock reset. The driver writes the Configuration word last to keep that window short. Choose Mode::Shutdown in the defaults to avoid it.
docs.title: A20: programming the power-on defaults with continuous mode

docs.text: With EUN = 1 every write to a programmable register is stored in EEPROM (7.5.1.2, p. 18, Table 7-10, p. 30), and EUN is cleared only by a general-call reset or a power cycle (and, by A6 , perhaps by a write of 0). A host that restarts during ProgramPowerOnDefaults() , or a lock that failed and was left to a power cycle, leaves the chip unlocked while the driver starts again with no memory of it. Writing the limits, the offset and the configuration would program them as power-on defaults, and every later setter would program EEPROM again (1000 writes minimum endurance, section 6.6). What the driver does: after Device_ID and before its first register write, EnsureInitialized() reads EEPROM_UL. With EUN = 1 it writes EUN = 0 and reads it back (up to three times, as in the relock). If EUN still reads 1 the call returns EepromVerifyFailed (or the bus error of the failed write) and has written nothing else; the application power-cycles the chip or sends the general-call reset itself. Start-up never writes anything else without a confirmed lock. A lock is confirmed only by a clean read-back with EUN = 0: a reply that breaks bits 13:0 is no lock, at start-up as in the relock after programming, even when its EUN bit reads 0. Switch-off is different, because never switching the chip off is the worse failure (RD-05). Its rules are the switch-off decision table . When the driver is not initialised, Deinitialize() and SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) read EEPROM_UL once. EUN = 0 on a clean reply: the shutdown write is sent. Otherwise (EUN = 1, a failed read, or a reply that breaks bits 13:0) the driver writes EUN = 0 and reads it back, at most twice; the lock write programs no EEPROM. Only the read after the last lock write decides: when it is clean and shows EUN = 1, the lock cannot be cleared and the write would be programmed as a power-on default of "shutdown" (the chip would then need a power cycle anyway), so it is refused with EepromVerifyFailed and nothing is sent. A clean EUN = 1 seen before a later lock write is stale and never refuses; a failed or garbled read is no evidence. A chip that answers neither the first read nor the lock write gets nothing more ( Bus ). The residual risk is stated: if every lock write was lost or did not take and no read-back succeeded, the shutdown word is programmed. No write follows a clean EEPROM_UL reply with EEPROM_Busy set (the power-up load or a word being programmed): the driver waits 7 ms and reads again, twice at most, and returns Timeout with nothing sent when the chip is still busy. The whole call makes at most 8 transfers and waits at most 14 ms. An initialised driver is always locked (it became initialised only after a confirmed lock), so its switch-off needs no extra read, unless its settle finds reset evidence (row I3). Two residual risks are stated in the contract : row U5 above, and one bit flipped on the bus in the first EEPROM_UL reply of an unlocked chip (EUN read as 0 with bits 13:0 clean). The bus has no CRC, so the driver takes that reply for a lock and writes one word: start-up programs one limit as a power-on default and then fails its read-back, switch-off row U1 programs the shutdown word. It needs an interrupted programming and a bus error on exactly that read; the cost is one EEPROM word. Knob: the model's ForceUnlock() leaves EUN set as an interrupted programming does; eun_write_zero_locks = false makes the lock write ineffective. Bench step, not hardware-verified: interrupt a programming and read EEPROM_UL at the next start.
docs.title: A21: start-up and switch-off on an unlocked chip

docs.text: 7.5.1.1 names only the limit registers and Configuration as ignored during the load; it says nothing about a write to EEPROM_UL then, or about whether EUN reads valid while EEPROM_Busy is set. The switch-off writes nothing after a busy EEPROM_UL reply and reads again after the wait, so neither answer changes what it does. A lock write after a failed read (no evidence) may still land in a load; it programs nothing either way. Knob: none. Bench step, not hardware-verified: power-cycle the chip and read EEPROM_UL within 1 ms.
docs.title: A22: EEPROM_UL during the power-up load

docs.text: tests/test_faults.cpp runs a whole session (start, set limits and alert function, read, one-shot, program a user word, deinitialise) under each reading above and checks that the driver never wrote while the chip was loading or busy, never wrote a traceability or read-only register or an undefined pointer, and never left the EEPROM unlocked. That session waits out every load it causes; the switch-off rows W1, I3 and R1 in tests/test_switch_off.cpp switch off inside the load, with no time passing, under both readings of A14. tests/test_eeprom.cpp covers A2, A5 and A6 in both readings and every failure path of the relock; tests/test_safety_regressions.cpp covers A19 and A21 in both readings, and tests/test_switch_off.cpp every row of the switch-off decision table.

docs.text: API guide ¶ The driver's API by task, with code that compiles: initialise, configure, measure, handle errors and shut down. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Texas Instruments SNOSD82D D: Power-up, the EEPROM load and the first result: 7.3.1 Power-Up, p. 12 Result format, LSB and the 8000h value: 7.3.3 Temperature Result and Limits; Table 7-1, p. 13 Continuous, shutdown and one-shot modes: 7.4.1 Continuous Conversion; 7.4.2 Shutdown; 7.4.3 One-Shot, p. 14 Alert mode and therm mode: 7.4.4 Therm and Alert Modes, p. 15 EEPROM, unlock and programming: 7.5.1 EEPROM Overview, p. 18 Traceability words that must not be erased: 7.5.1.1 EEPROM Overview; 7.5.1.2 Programming the EEPROM; 7.6.7 EEPROM1; 7.6.10 EEPROM3, p. 18 SMBus alert response and general call: 7.5.3.1.5 SMBus Alert Function; 7.5.3.1.6 General-Call Reset Function, p. 22 Configuration register: 7.6.3 Configuration Register; Table 7-6, p. 27 Averaging and the conversion cycle time: 7.3.2 Averaging; Table 7-7, p. 28 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The shape of the API ¶ Group Calls Lifecycle EnsureInitialized() , IsInitialized() , Deinitialize() , SoftReset() , GeneralCallReset() Configuration Configure() , GetConfig() , SetMode() , SetAveraging() , SetCycleTime() , SetAlertFunction() , SetAlertPolarity() , SetAlertSource() , SetLimits() , SetOffsetMilliC() Measurement ReadTemperatureMilliC() , ReadTemperatureRaw() , StartOneShot() , ReadOneShotMilliC() , WaitDataReady() Status and alerts ReadStatus() , GetLatchedStatus() , ClearLatchedStatus() , ReadAlertPin() EEPROM ProgramPowerOnDefaults() , ProgramUserWord() , ReadUniqueId() Diagnostics CheckHealth() , ReadRegister() , GetLastConfigWord() , GetRevision() , tmp117::GetDriverVersion() Not covered SmbusAlertResponse() always returns Unsupported ( Ambiguities ) Every call that touches the chip returns Result<T> : check ok() (or the bool conversion) and read value , or read error . Result is [[nodiscard]] , so an unchecked call is a compiler warning. A failed call holds T{} . Initialise ¶ tmp117 :: Error BringUp ( Sensor & sensor ) { // The one entry point: waits for the power-up load, checks Device_ID, writes the configuration // and reads it back. After a failure the next call starts again from the beginning. const auto r = sensor . EnsureInitialized (); if ( ! r ) { std :: printf ( "TMP117 init: %s \n " , tmp117 :: ToString ( r . error )); } return r . error ; } The constructor stores the port, the address and the configuration ( Config{} unless you pass one) and does no I/O. EnsureInitialized() is the one way to start the chip. Its first call brings the bus up, waits for the chip's power-up load (about 1.5 ms, then a bounded poll of EEPROM_Busy, see Config::reset_timeout_ms ), checks that Device_ID reads 0x117 in bits 11:0, writes the limits, the offset and the configuration, and reads them back. It does not reset the chip: the chip is in the state its EEPROM gives it and the configuration is written over it. Once it has succeeded, EnsureInitialized() returns Ok at once with no I/O, so a caller can call it before every use. After a failure the driver stays uninitialised and the next call starts again from the beginning. No other call starts the chip: before EnsureInitialized() succeeds every read and write returns NotInitialized and sends nothing, and Configure() and the setters do not store anything either. To change the start-up settings, pass them to the constructor. The Device_ID check masks the revision field (bits 15:12) and compares bits 11:0 with 0x117 , so a TMP117 of any silicon revision passes, and a TMP119 (ID 0x2117 ) reads as revision 2 of a TMP117: see Ambiguities . Read continuously ¶ In Mode::Continuous (the reset value) the chip converts on its own cycle and ReadTemperatureMilliC() returns the latest result in thousandths of a degree Celsius, rounded half away from zero. One count is 7.8125 m°C, so ReadTemperatureRaw() gives the counts for code that wants to avoid the multiplication. The result 8000h (-256 °C) is never returned as a temperature. Before the first conversion after the start it means "no result yet" and the call returns NoMeasurement : wait one cycle ( GetCycleTimeUs() gives it from the settings) and ask again. After the driver has seen a real result, 8000h can only mean the chip restarted, and the call returns UnexpectedReset . A continuous read does not tell a fresh result from an old one. ReadStatus().value.data_ready says that a conversion finished since the last read of Configuration or Temp_Result. Verify::Device reads Device_ID before the temperature, one more transfer. A data line stuck at all zeros or all ones cannot pass it, so use it when the temperature feeds a decision and the bus is long or noisy. Without it, a result of 0000h or FFFFh (what a stuck line returns, and also 0 degC and -1 count on a working chip) is confirmed by a Device_ID read before it is returned, so those two values cost one more transfer and a stuck line fails with DeviceIdMismatch . A line that repeats a word other than these two is not caught without Verify::Device . Measure on demand ¶ Shutdown between samples keeps the chip at about 0.15 µA. ReadOneShotMilliC() starts one conversion, waits for the time the averaging setting needs, and reads the result: tmp117 :: Result < int32_t > SampleOnDemand ( Sensor & sensor ) { // Shutdown between samples: the chip draws about 0.15 uA while it waits. return sensor . ReadOneShotMilliC (); // start, wait for Data_Ready, read, back to shutdown } The wait is (conversions + 1) x 17.5 ms , one conversion more than needed as margin for the oscillator, which the datasheet does not give an accuracy for: 35 ms for one conversion up to 1.14 s for 64. If the chip does not finish, the call sends shutdown and returns Timeout . StartOneShot() and WaitDataReady() are the two halves for code that does something else meanwhile; while a one-shot is pending the setters and ReadTemperature*() return Busy , except SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) , which ends it. ReadOneShotMilliC() leaves the chip in shutdown, also when the driver was in continuous mode, and GetConfig().mode says Shutdown afterwards: ReadTemperatureMilliC() then returns the last result for ever, with no error. Call SetMode(Mode::Continuous) to resume continuous conversion. Alerts ¶ tmp117 :: Error ArmOverTemperature ( Sensor & sensor ) { // Window mode: ALERT is active (low) outside -20 degC .. 85 degC. A low above a high is refused // before any frame is sent. if ( auto r = sensor . SetAlertFunction ( tmp117 :: AlertFunction :: Window ); ! r ) { return r . error ; } return sensor . SetLimits ( -20000 , 85000 ). error ; } Alert mode ( AlertFunction::Window ): ALERT is active when a result is above the high limit or below the low limit, and the flags stay set until Configuration is read. Therm mode ( AlertFunction::Threshold ): ALERT is active above the high limit and stays active until the result is below the low limit, so the two limits make a hysteresis. In both modes SetLimits() takes both limits at once in thousandths of a degree, refuses a value outside -256000 to 255992 and refuses a low above the high ( Ambiguities ). Nothing is clamped. The chip clears HIGH_Alert, LOW_Alert and Data_Ready every time Configuration is read. The driver reads Configuration itself (to check for a reset, to wait), so it keeps what it saw: bool OverTemperatureSeen ( Sensor & sensor ) { // The flags clear on every read of the Configuration register, so the driver latches them: this // returns what was seen since the last ClearLatchedStatus(). const auto s = sensor . ReadStatus (); return s && ( s . value . high_alert || sensor . GetLatchedStatus (). high_alert ); } GetLatchedStatus() returns every flag any read has seen since ClearLatchedStatus() . The driver's own reads release the ALERT pin. In alert mode a read of Configuration clears HIGH_Alert and LOW_Alert and so deasserts ALERT (7.4.4.1, p. 16). ReadStatus() , WaitDataReady() , StartOneShot() , CheckHealth() , the settle reads after a failed write and a raw ReadRegister() of Configuration all read it, so an application that services ALERT as a level interrupt can find the pin released by the driver's own polling. The flags are not lost: they are in GetLatchedStatus() , which an interrupt service routine should consult rather than the pin. Poll less, or do not poll while a level interrupt is pending, if the pin itself must stay asserted until your handler has run. In therm mode the flag follows the limits and a read does not clear it. ReadAlertPin() returns the level of the ALERT pin after polarity, true while the pin is active, and needs the optional ReadAlertPin() hook of the port; without it the call returns Unsupported . Handle errors ¶ const char * Describe ( tmp117 :: Error e ) { switch ( e ) { case tmp117 :: Error :: Bus : case tmp117 :: Error :: DeviceIdMismatch : return "check the bus wiring and the address pin" ; case tmp117 :: Error :: UnexpectedReset : return "the chip restarted: call EnsureInitialized() again, check the supply" ; case tmp117 :: Error :: NoMeasurement : return "no result yet: wait one conversion cycle" ; default : return tmp117 :: ToString ( e ); } } Signal Meaning What to do Error::Bus The port failed a transfer Check the port and the wiring; retry, or Deinitialize() and EnsureInitialized() Error::Timeout The power-up load, a conversion or an EEPROM word did not finish in time Check V+ and the pull-ups; raise the deadline in Config if the part is slow. From a switch-off: the EEPROM was still busy after 14 ms and nothing was sent; call it again Error::DeviceIdMismatch Device_ID is not 0x117 in bits 11:0 Check the address pin and the wiring; another device may answer. A switch-off after it sends nothing to that device Error::BadReply A bit that must read 0 reads 1, or a register does not read back what was written A noisy or stuck line; lower the clock, check the pull-ups Error::NoMeasurement No conversion has finished since the start Wait one cycle and read again Error::UnexpectedReset The chip restarted behind the driver's back Check the supply; EnsureInitialized() starts it again. To switch it off instead, call Deinitialize() at once: it waits out the chip's power-up load (up to 14 ms); on Timeout call it again Error::EepromVerifyFailed The EEPROM did not hold what was written, or it could not be relocked Power-cycle the chip, then read the registers before trusting it Error::Busy A one-shot is pending Wait for it, or SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) Error::Unsupported ReadAlertPin() without the hook, GeneralCallReset() without the opt-in, SmbusAlertResponse() Add the hook, set allow_general_call , or read ReadStatus() Error::InvalidArgument An argument is out of range Nothing was sent; fix the argument Crc and DeviceFault belong to the base set that every driver of the family shares; the TMP117 has no CRC on its bus and reports no sensing fault, so this driver never returns them. Every value, with the calls that return it, is on the Contract page. tmp117::ToString() names an error for a log. Check that the chip is still the one you started ¶ CheckHealth() reads Device_ID and Configuration and compares the setting fields with the driver's copy. It returns UnexpectedReset when the chip no longer holds them. A reset to exactly the values the driver wrote is invisible without a reset flag (ambiguity A9); only a result of 8000h after a real one gives it away. Diagnostics ¶ For bring-up and fault finding: Call I/O What it gives ReadRegister(pointer) one transfer, no retry The raw word of one register of the map (00h to 08h and 0Fh); other pointers return InvalidArgument and send nothing GetLastConfigWord() none The raw Configuration word of the last read, by any call GetLatchedStatus() none The alert and data-ready flags of every Configuration read since the last ClearLatchedStatus() ReadUniqueId() three transfers EEPROM1, EEPROM2 and EEPROM3; the first and third hold the traceability identifier GetRevision() none The revision field of Device_ID read at the start Program the power-on defaults ¶ The chip loads its configuration, limits and offset from its EEPROM at power-up, so a chip that must start in a known state without a host (a thermostat that guards a load) can be programmed once: tmp117 :: Config defaults {}; defaults . low_limit_mc = 5000 ; // alert below 5 degC defaults . high_limit_mc = 60000 ; // alert above 60 degC const auto r = sensor . ProgramPowerOnDefaults ( defaults ); // r.error: Ok, or EepromVerifyFailed, Timeout, Bus, BadReply, InvalidArgument, Busy This is a guarded operation, never started by another call. It shuts the chip down, unlocks the EEPROM, writes each word and waits for it, locks the EEPROM again, resets the chip, checks that the lock is off, reads the words back and starts the running configuration. EEPROM1 and EEPROM3, the NIST traceability words the datasheet says not to erase, are never written: the driver refuses their pointers and checks, before and after, that they are unchanged. The EEPROM endurance is 1000 writes, so do not call it in a loop. After any error the driver is uninitialised and the chip's state is unknown: read the registers, power-cycle if the error is EepromVerifyFailed , and start again. Ambiguities says what the datasheet leaves open about the relock and what the verification can and cannot prove. ProgramUserWord() writes the user word EEPROM2 the same way. Shut down ¶ void PowerDown ( Sensor & sensor ) { // Always sends shutdown, even if the driver believes the chip is already there. if ( auto r = sensor . Deinitialize (); ! r ) { std :: printf ( "TMP117 shutdown write failed: %s \n " , tmp117 :: ToString ( r . error )); } } Deinitialize() sends the shutdown write whatever doubt the driver holds, and marks the driver uninitialised even if the write failed. After the driver lost track of the chip it reads EEPROM_UL first and sends nothing while the chip is busy (its power-up load, or a word being programmed): it waits 7 ms and reads again, twice at most, and returns Timeout when the chip is still busy (call it again). It then writes the EEPROM lock, and it sends nothing when the read after its last lock write shows EUN = 1 ( EepromVerifyFailed ; power-cycle the chip, A21). After a Device_ID mismatch it sends nothing to another device ( DeviceIdMismatch ). The rules are the switch-off decision table . After it every call returns NotInitialized until the next EnsureInitialized() , which starts the chip again from the beginning: Deinitialize() then EnsureInitialized() is also the recovery after a fault. Two calls still reach the chip in that state, because a driver that lost track of it must be able to switch it off: Deinitialize() and SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) . On a driver that never reached the chip (no EnsureInitialized() yet, or one refused for an argument or a port that did not come up) Deinitialize() returns Ok and sends nothing: it does not switch off a chip that converts from its power-on defaults (row N1), and SetMode() returns NotInitialized . Next: Configuration .

The flags are not lost: they are in GetLatchedStatus() , which an interrupt service routine should consult rather than the pin. Poll less, or do not poll while a level interrupt is pending, if the pin itself must stay asserted until your handler has run. In therm mode the flag follows the limits and a read does not clear it. ReadAlertPin() returns the level of the ALERT pin after polarity, true while the pin is active, and needs the optional ReadAlertPin() hook of the port; without it the call returns Unsupported .
docs.title: Alerts

docs.text: const char * Describe ( tmp117 :: Error e ) { switch ( e ) { case tmp117 :: Error :: Bus : case tmp117 :: Error :: DeviceIdMismatch : return "check the bus wiring and the address pin" ; case tmp117 :: Error :: UnexpectedReset : return "the chip restarted: call EnsureInitialized() again, check the supply" ; case tmp117 :: Error :: NoMeasurement : return "no result yet: wait one conversion cycle" ; default : return tmp117 :: ToString ( e ); } } Signal Meaning What to do Error::Bus The port failed a transfer Check the port and the wiring; retry, or Deinitialize() and EnsureInitialized() Error::Timeout The power-up load, a conversion or an EEPROM word did not finish in time Check V+ and the pull-ups; raise the deadline in Config if the part is slow. From a switch-off: the EEPROM was still busy after 14 ms and nothing was sent; call it again Error::DeviceIdMismatch Device_ID is not 0x117 in bits 11:0 Check the address pin and the wiring; another device may answer. A switch-off after it sends nothing to that device Error::BadReply A bit that must read 0 reads 1, or a register does not read back what was written A noisy or stuck line; lower the clock, check the pull-ups Error::NoMeasurement No conversion has finished since the start Wait one cycle and read again Error::UnexpectedReset The chip restarted behind the driver's back Check the supply; EnsureInitialized() starts it again. To switch it off instead, call Deinitialize() at once: it waits out the chip's power-up load (up to 14 ms); on Timeout call it again Error::EepromVerifyFailed The EEPROM did not hold what was written, or it could not be relocked Power-cycle the chip, then read the registers before trusting it Error::Busy A one-shot is pending Wait for it, or SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) Error::Unsupported ReadAlertPin() without the hook, GeneralCallReset() without the opt-in, SmbusAlertResponse() Add the hook, set allow_general_call , or read ReadStatus() Error::InvalidArgument An argument is out of range Nothing was sent; fix the argument Crc and DeviceFault belong to the base set that every driver of the family shares; the TMP117 has no CRC on its bus and reports no sensing fault, so this driver never returns them. Every value, with the calls that return it, is on the Contract page. tmp117::ToString() names an error for a log.

docs.text: CheckHealth() reads Device_ID and Configuration and compares the setting fields with the driver's copy. It returns UnexpectedReset when the chip no longer holds them. A reset to exactly the values the driver wrote is invisible without a reset flag (ambiguity A9); only a result of 8000h after a real one gives it away.
