docs.text: The chip loads its configuration, limits and offset from its EEPROM at power-up, so a chip that must start in a known state without a host (a thermostat that guards a load) can be programmed once: tmp117 :: Config defaults {}; defaults . low_limit_mc = 5000 ; // alert below 5 degC defaults . high_limit_mc = 60000 ; // alert above 60 degC const auto r = sensor . ProgramPowerOnDefaults ( defaults ); // r.error: Ok, or EepromVerifyFailed, Timeout, Bus, BadReply, InvalidArgument, Busy This is a guarded operation, never started by another call. It shuts the chip down, unlocks the EEPROM, writes each word and waits for it, locks the EEPROM again, resets the chip, checks that the lock is off, reads the words back and starts the running configuration. EEPROM1 and EEPROM3, the NIST traceability words the datasheet says not to erase, are never written: the driver refuses their pointers and checks, before and after, that they are unchanged. The EEPROM endurance is 1000 writes, so do not call it in a loop. After any error the driver is uninitialised and the chip's state is unknown: read the registers, power-cycle if the error is EepromVerifyFailed , and start again. Ambiguities says what the datasheet leaves open about the relock and what the verification can and cannot prove. ProgramUserWord() writes the user word EEPROM2 the same way.
docs.title: Program the power-on defaults

docs.text: void PowerDown ( Sensor & sensor ) { // Always sends shutdown, even if the driver believes the chip is already there. if ( auto r = sensor . Deinitialize (); ! r ) { std :: printf ( "TMP117 shutdown write failed: %s \n " , tmp117 :: ToString ( r . error )); } } Deinitialize() sends the shutdown write whatever doubt the driver holds, and marks the driver uninitialised even if the write failed. After the driver lost track of the chip it reads EEPROM_UL first and sends nothing while the chip is busy (its power-up load, or a word being programmed): it waits 7 ms and reads again, twice at most, and returns Timeout when the chip is still busy (call it again). It then writes the EEPROM lock, and it sends nothing when the read after its last lock write shows EUN = 1 ( EepromVerifyFailed ; power-cycle the chip, A21). After a Device_ID mismatch it sends nothing to another device ( DeviceIdMismatch ). The rules are the switch-off decision table . After it every call returns NotInitialized until the next EnsureInitialized() , which starts the chip again from the beginning: Deinitialize() then EnsureInitialized() is also the recovery after a fault. Two calls still reach the chip in that state, because a driver that lost track of it must be able to switch it off: Deinitialize() and SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) . On a driver that never reached the chip (no EnsureInitialized() yet, or one refused for an argument or a port that did not come up) Deinitialize() returns Ok and sends nothing: it does not switch off a chip that converts from its power-on defaults (row N1), and SetMode() returns NotInitialized . Next: Configuration .

docs.text: Architecture ¶ How the driver is built: three layers, one of them yours, and what happens in each when you read a temperature. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Texas Instruments SNOSD82D D: Result format, LSB and the 8000h value: 7.3.3 Temperature Result and Limits; Table 7-1, p. 13 Register map and reset values: 7.6 Register Map; Table 7-3, p. 25 Configuration register: 7.6.3 Configuration Register; Table 7-6, p. 27 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your application calls one object, whose public calls are listed from the umbrella header in inc/. The core turns each call into register reads and writes and hands them to the port contract (the CRTP base in inc/*_interface.hpp), which forwards them, at compile time, to the hooks of the port class you write; your port moves the bytes on the bus. The notes on the right say which layers stay the same on every MCU and which one you write. A library without a port contract has only the first two layers. Drawn from: inc/tmp117.hpp public calls ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp I2cInterface ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . Layers ¶ Layer Files Owns Core inc/tmp117.hpp , src/tmp117.ipp Lifecycle, the shadow of the chip's registers, conversions, the flag latch, reset evidence, the EEPROM sequence, timeouts, errors Types and registers inc/tmp117_types.hpp , inc/tmp117_registers.hpp Error , Result<T> , Config , the cycle-time table, unit conversion; the register map and the bit fields Port contract inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp The CRTP base, the I2cPort concept, the bus requirements, RegisterBus (pointer and word framing) Platform port Your class Bus bring-up and byte transfers, the delay, optionally the ALERT pin and logging Kconfig layer inc/tmp117_kconfig.hpp Optional: a Config from ESP-IDF menuconfig One call through the layers ¶ One call through the layers Figure description and sources Three participants: your code, the core class TMP117 and your port. Your code calls ReadTemperatureMilliC. The core asks the port to write the pointer and read two bytes. A result of 8000h before any conversion ends the call with NoMeasurement, and after one it is evidence of a reset. Otherwise the core multiplies the counts by 7.8125 and returns a Result holding the value 23456 and the status Ok to your code. Drawn from: docs/model/read-call.seq.yml . Design choices ¶ CRTP, not virtual functions. The port is a template parameter constrained by the I2cPort concept, so every call is resolved at compile time and a missing hook is a compile error that names it. Optional hooks by requires . DelayUs , ReadAlertPin and Log are detected with C++20 requires in one place. A missing DelayUs() fails to compile, a missing ReadAlertPin() makes the driver call return Unsupported , a missing Log() logs nothing; none is skipped silently. A shadow of the chip, adopted only after the chip accepted. The driver keeps the configuration it believes the chip holds. A write that fails goes into a "doubt" mask; the next call reads the register back and keeps whichever of the old and the attempted value the chip shows. A value that is neither is a reset. Reset evidence instead of a reset flag. The chip has no power-on flag. The driver treats three things as a reset: the configuration setting bits differ from the shadow, EEPROM_Busy is set when the driver did not start a programming, or the result reads 8000h after a real one. It then stops sending writes and returns UnexpectedReset ( Contract ). One writer for every register. RegisterBus::WriteWord refuses the pointers of the read-only registers and of the two traceability words, so no code path can erase them. Member buffers. Transfer buffers are members of the driver, never stack arrays handed to an asynchronous port. No I/O in the constructor. Construction cannot fail, so the driver can be a static or a member of a handler. One error type. Result<T> carries a value and an Error ; nothing throws and nothing returns a bare bool . No heap, no exceptions, no RTTI, no std::function , no printf . The driver is a header-only template with no mutable static state. docs.text: On the bus ¶ What the TMP117 needs from the bus, signal by signal, with every time and rate taken from the datasheet. The register framing is on the Hardware page; this page is the waveform under it. I2C timing ¶ The TMP117 is an I2C target at the address its ADD0 pin selects. Data changes while SCL is low and is read while SCL is high; a start or a stop is SDA changing while SCL is high. I2C timing of the address byte Figure description and sources The two lanes are SCL and SDA, left to right in time. SDA falls while SCL is high (the start), the address bits follow, each stable while SCL is high, then the TMP117 pulls SDA low for the acknowledge. The table under the lanes gives each interval with its datasheet value. Drawn from: docs/model/bus-timing.timing.yml . Several devices ¶ Up to four TMP117 share one bus, each at the address its ADD0 pin selects. Up to four TMP117 on one I2C bus Figure description and sources The MCU on top and the TMP117 devices under it connect to the rails SDA and SCL on the right; the dashed card stands for the devices in between. One pull-up per line ties the bus to the supply. Drawn from: docs/model/bus-topology.topology.yml . How these figures are made ¶ Each figure is a model in docs/model/ ( bus-timing.timing.yml , and bus-topology.topology.yml when the chip shares a bus) that cites the datasheet section and page of every number; kokeb-docs figures draws it and the build fails on a number without a citation. The values table under each waveform is also written as docs/diagrams/<id>.table.html .

docs.text: Changelog ¶ What changed in each release of the driver. Entries under Breaking need source changes in code that used the affected API. [Unreleased] ¶ Added ¶ First version of the TMP117 driver (Texas Instruments TMP117, I2C), written from datasheet SNOSD82D Rev. D. Start-up that waits for the power-up load, checks Device_ID (any revision), writes the limits, the offset and the configuration and reads them back. Continuous, shutdown and one-shot conversion, averaging of 1, 8, 32 or 64 conversions, the eight cycle times of Table 7-7 as data, alert and therm mode, ALERT polarity and source, limits and offset in thousandths of a degree. A latch for the flags the chip clears on read, reset evidence without a reset flag, and a settle step after a failed write. Start-up reads EEPROM_UL and locks an unlocked chip before its first write, and refuses (writing nothing else) when the lock cannot be confirmed; switch-off sends even when settling a write in doubt failed. Switch-off follows one decision table (docs/contract.md): an uninitialised driver writes the EEPROM lock and sends the shutdown write unless the read after its last lock write is clean with EUN = 1 (A21); a failed, garbled or earlier read never refuses. No write follows an EEPROM_UL reply that shows the power-up load or a word being programmed: two 7 ms waits at most, then Timeout with nothing sent. A settle that finds a reset hands over to these rows, and after a Device_ID mismatch nothing is sent to another device. At most 8 transfers (9 after a mismatch) and 14 ms; a chip that answers nothing costs 2 transfers. A settle read that shows EEPROM_Busy counts as reset evidence. The code builds on GCC 10 and Clang 13 (no <bit> ). A failed shutdown write while a one-shot runs is settled as "not taken", not as a reset. A one-shot counts as complete when Data_Ready was seen or MOD reads shutdown, so either reading of ambiguity A19 works; ReadStatus() confirms a reply of 0000h with Device_ID. A guarded EEPROM path ( ProgramPowerOnDefaults() , ProgramUserWord() ) that relocks on every failure path and never writes the two traceability words. An optional ReadAlertPin() hook, GeneralCallReset() behind an explicit opt-in, and a documented list of the datasheet's ambiguities with the model switch that tests each reading. Host tests against a register model written from the datasheet, a fuzz target, a host example, an ESP-IDF example and the documentation site with its figures. Not included: the SMBus alert response (returns Unsupported ), the TMP116 and TMP119, any run on hardware.

docs.text: Configuration ¶ Every field of tmp117::Config , the presets, how a configuration is checked, and the optional Kconfig layer. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Texas Instruments SNOSD82D D: Continuous, shutdown and one-shot modes: 7.4.1 Continuous Conversion; 7.4.2 Shutdown; 7.4.3 One-Shot, p. 14 Alert mode and therm mode: 7.4.4 Therm and Alert Modes, p. 15 Register map and reset values: 7.6 Register Map; Table 7-3, p. 25 Averaging and the conversion cycle time: 7.3.2 Averaging; Table 7-7, p. 28 Limit registers and the offset register: 7.6.4 THigh_Limit; 7.6.5 TLow_Limit (p. 29); 7.6.9 Temperature Offset (p. 31), p. 29 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . Fields ¶ Config{} holds the chip's reset values, so it changes nothing on a freshly reset chip. Fields with a unit carry it in the name. Temperatures are integers in thousandths of a degree Celsius; the chip's step is 7.8125 m°C, so a value is rounded half away from zero to the nearest step. Field Default Range Register mode Mode::Continuous Continuous , Shutdown Configuration MOD averaging Averaging::X8 X1 , X8 , X32 , X64 Configuration AVG cycle_time CycleTime::S1 Ms15p5 , Ms125 , Ms250 , Ms500 , S1 , S4 , S8 , S16 Configuration CONV alert_function AlertFunction::Window Window (alert mode), Threshold (therm mode) Configuration T/nA alert_polarity AlertPolarity::ActiveLow ActiveLow , ActiveHigh Configuration POL alert_source AlertSource::Flags Flags , DataReady Configuration DR/Alert low_limit_mc -256000 -256000 to high_limit_mc TLow_Limit high_limit_mc 192000 low_limit_mc to 255992 THigh_Limit offset_mc 0 -256000 to 255992 Temp_Offset reset_timeout_ms 10 1 to 1000 driver only: the longest wait for the power-up load eeprom_timeout_ms 50 1 to 1000 driver only: the longest wait for one EEPROM word allow_general_call false driver only: opt in to the bus-wide reset The one-shot mode is not a Mode : a one-shot is an action ( StartOneShot() , ReadOneShotMilliC() ), and the chip cannot store it in EEPROM. The datasheet's second continuous code (MOD 10) reads back as 00 and is never written. The defaults for the two deadlines are the driver's choice, because the datasheet gives only typical values (about 1.5 ms for the power-up load and about 7 ms for an EEPROM word): see A1 and A2 . The cycle time of a setting is in Table 7-7 and in GetCycleTimeUs(cycle_time, averaging) : the longer of the CONV time and the averaging time, so CycleTime::Ms15p5 with Averaging::X8 runs at 125 ms. Choosing a setting ¶ You want Set The lowest power at one result per second the defaults; Mode::Shutdown between ReadOneShotMilliC() calls for less The lowest noise Averaging::X32 or X64 ; the cycle becomes at least 0.5 s or 1 s The fastest result Averaging::X1 , CycleTime::Ms15p5 ; one result every 15.5 ms An alert that stays on until it cools AlertFunction::Threshold with the low limit below the high limit ALERT as a "new result" interrupt AlertSource::DataReady The chip heats itself by a few millidegrees when it converts all the time, which is why a long cycle with shutdown between conversions measures the surroundings better. The datasheet's section 8.2.2.2 gives the numbers. Start from Config{} and change fields: tmp117 :: Config LowNoiseConfig () { tmp117 :: Config c {}; // datasheet reset values c . averaging = tmp117 :: Averaging :: X32 ; c . cycle_time = tmp117 :: CycleTime :: S1 ; // 32 conversions need at least 1 s: Table 7-7 c . low_limit_mc = 5000 ; // alert below 5 degC c . high_limit_mc = 60000 ; // alert above 60 degC c . offset_mc = -250 ; // a measured board offset, subtracted by the chip return c ; // tmp117::Validate(c) checks it without the chip } tmp117 :: Error StartLowNoise ( MyPort & port ) { static tmp117 :: TMP117 < MyPort > sensor ( port , LowNoiseConfig ()); // stored, no I/O return sensor . EnsureInitialized (). error ; // InvalidArgument if low is above high } Validation ¶ tmp117::Validate(config) checks a configuration without touching the chip, and EnsureInitialized() and Configure() call it before any I/O. It returns Error::InvalidArgument when an enum holds a value that is not an enumerator, a limit or the offset is outside -256000 to 255992 m°C, the low limit is above the high limit, or a deadline is zero or above 1000 ms. CheckedConfig does the same at build time: a constant configuration that fails does not compile ( compile-fail test ). Kconfig ¶ Under ESP-IDF, idf.py menuconfig shows TMP117 temperature sensor when the driver is a component of the project ( Installation ); the menu is _config/Kconfig . The options reach the code only through inc/tmp117_kconfig.hpp , never through a driver signature: tmp117 :: Error StartFromMenuconfig ( MyPort & port ) { static tmp117 :: TMP117 < MyPort > sensor ( port , tmp117 :: KconfigDefaults ()); return sensor . EnsureInitialized (). error ; } Option Default Config field CONFIG_TMP117_AVERAGING_* 8 averaging CONFIG_TMP117_CYCLE_* 1 s cycle_time CONFIG_TMP117_RESET_TIMEOUT_MS 10 reset_timeout_ms CONFIG_TMP117_EEPROM_TIMEOUT_MS 50 eeprom_timeout_ms The limits, the offset and the general-call opt-in are deliberately not menu options: a wrong alert limit is a decision about the system, not a build setting. Without Kconfig (plain CMake, other platforms) KconfigDefaults() returns Config{} . Both cases are host tests. Next: Porting .

docs.text: Every field of tmp117::Config , the presets, how a configuration is checked, and the optional Kconfig layer. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Texas Instruments SNOSD82D D: Continuous, shutdown and one-shot modes: 7.4.1 Continuous Conversion; 7.4.2 Shutdown; 7.4.3 One-Shot, p. 14 Alert mode and therm mode: 7.4.4 Therm and Alert Modes, p. 15 Register map and reset values: 7.6 Register Map; Table 7-3, p. 25 Averaging and the conversion cycle time: 7.3.2 Averaging; Table 7-7, p. 28 Limit registers and the offset register: 7.6.4 THigh_Limit; 7.6.5 TLow_Limit (p. 29); 7.6.9 Temperature Offset (p. 31), p. 29 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map .
docs.title: Configuration

docs.text: Config{} holds the chip's reset values, so it changes nothing on a freshly reset chip. Fields with a unit carry it in the name. Temperatures are integers in thousandths of a degree Celsius; the chip's step is 7.8125 m°C, so a value is rounded half away from zero to the nearest step. Field Default Range Register mode Mode::Continuous Continuous , Shutdown Configuration MOD averaging Averaging::X8 X1 , X8 , X32 , X64 Configuration AVG cycle_time CycleTime::S1 Ms15p5 , Ms125 , Ms250 , Ms500 , S1 , S4 , S8 , S16 Configuration CONV alert_function AlertFunction::Window Window (alert mode), Threshold (therm mode) Configuration T/nA alert_polarity AlertPolarity::ActiveLow ActiveLow , ActiveHigh Configuration POL alert_source AlertSource::Flags Flags , DataReady Configuration DR/Alert low_limit_mc -256000 -256000 to high_limit_mc TLow_Limit high_limit_mc 192000 low_limit_mc to 255992 THigh_Limit offset_mc 0 -256000 to 255992 Temp_Offset reset_timeout_ms 10 1 to 1000 driver only: the longest wait for the power-up load eeprom_timeout_ms 50 1 to 1000 driver only: the longest wait for one EEPROM word allow_general_call false driver only: opt in to the bus-wide reset The one-shot mode is not a Mode : a one-shot is an action ( StartOneShot() , ReadOneShotMilliC() ), and the chip cannot store it in EEPROM. The datasheet's second continuous code (MOD 10) reads back as 00 and is never written. The defaults for the two deadlines are the driver's choice, because the datasheet gives only typical values (about 1.5 ms for the power-up load and about 7 ms for an EEPROM word): see A1 and A2 . The cycle time of a setting is in Table 7-7 and in GetCycleTimeUs(cycle_time, averaging) : the longer of the CONV time and the averaging time, so CycleTime::Ms15p5 with Averaging::X8 runs at 125 ms.
docs.title: Fields

docs.text: You want Set The lowest power at one result per second the defaults; Mode::Shutdown between ReadOneShotMilliC() calls for less The lowest noise Averaging::X32 or X64 ; the cycle becomes at least 0.5 s or 1 s The fastest result Averaging::X1 , CycleTime::Ms15p5 ; one result every 15.5 ms An alert that stays on until it cools AlertFunction::Threshold with the low limit below the high limit ALERT as a "new result" interrupt AlertSource::DataReady The chip heats itself by a few millidegrees when it converts all the time, which is why a long cycle with shutdown between conversions measures the surroundings better. The datasheet's section 8.2.2.2 gives the numbers. Start from Config{} and change fields: tmp117 :: Config LowNoiseConfig () { tmp117 :: Config c {}; // datasheet reset values c . averaging = tmp117 :: Averaging :: X32 ; c . cycle_time = tmp117 :: CycleTime :: S1 ; // 32 conversions need at least 1 s: Table 7-7 c . low_limit_mc = 5000 ; // alert below 5 degC c . high_limit_mc = 60000 ; // alert above 60 degC c . offset_mc = -250 ; // a measured board offset, subtracted by the chip return c ; // tmp117::Validate(c) checks it without the chip } tmp117 :: Error StartLowNoise ( MyPort & port ) { static tmp117 :: TMP117 < MyPort > sensor ( port , LowNoiseConfig ()); // stored, no I/O return sensor . EnsureInitialized (). error ; // InvalidArgument if low is above high }
docs.title: Choosing a setting

docs.text: tmp117::Validate(config) checks a configuration without touching the chip, and EnsureInitialized() and Configure() call it before any I/O. It returns Error::InvalidArgument when an enum holds a value that is not an enumerator, a limit or the offset is outside -256000 to 255992 m°C, the low limit is above the high limit, or a deadline is zero or above 1000 ms. CheckedConfig does the same at build time: a constant configuration that fails does not compile ( compile-fail test ).
docs.title: Validation

docs.text: Under ESP-IDF, idf.py menuconfig shows TMP117 temperature sensor when the driver is a component of the project ( Installation ); the menu is _config/Kconfig . The options reach the code only through inc/tmp117_kconfig.hpp , never through a driver signature: tmp117 :: Error StartFromMenuconfig ( MyPort & port ) { static tmp117 :: TMP117 < MyPort > sensor ( port , tmp117 :: KconfigDefaults ()); return sensor . EnsureInitialized (). error ; } Option Default Config field CONFIG_TMP117_AVERAGING_* 8 averaging CONFIG_TMP117_CYCLE_* 1 s cycle_time CONFIG_TMP117_RESET_TIMEOUT_MS 10 reset_timeout_ms CONFIG_TMP117_EEPROM_TIMEOUT_MS 50 eeprom_timeout_ms The limits, the offset and the general-call opt-in are deliberately not menu options: a wrong alert limit is a decision about the system, not a build setting. Without Kconfig (plain CMake, other platforms) KconfigDefaults() returns Config{} . Both cases are host tests. Next: Porting .

docs.text: Contract ¶ What the TMP117 driver promises, what it needs, and the rules a caller follows. The driver inherits the Kokeb Labs driver contract ; this page states only what is specific to it. A change to anything here is a breaking change, listed under Breaking in the changelog . Promises ¶ The constructor is noexcept , stores the address and the configuration, does no I/O and cannot fail. EnsureInitialized() is the only way to start the driver. Its first call checks the address and the stored configuration ( InvalidArgument , nothing sent), brings the bus up, waits for the chip's power-up load, checks Device_ID, reads EEPROM_UL and locks the EEPROM when the unlock bit is set (see below), writes the limits, the offset and the configuration, and reads them back. On any failure the driver stays uninitialised and the next call starts again from the beginning; once it has succeeded, later calls return Ok with no I/O. Every call that touches the chip returns Error::NotInitialized before EnsureInitialized() succeeds and sends nothing. No call initialises or resets the chip as a side effect. An argument that is refused sends nothing. InvalidArgument is decided before the first transfer, in every call. The driver never writes a register it does not own. Temp_Result and Device_ID are read-only, and EEPROM1 and EEPROM3 hold the traceability identifier the datasheet says not to erase; RegisterBus::WriteWord refuses their pointers and every pointer outside the map. ProgramPowerOnDefaults() reads the two traceability words before and after and reports a change. The EEPROM is locked again on every path. ProgramPowerOnDefaults() and ProgramUserWord() never return with the unlock bit left set unless the chip refused to lock; then they return EepromVerifyFailed when that is the only failure, and the driver is uninitialised. After an earlier error (a Timeout of a word that never finished, a Bus error) the first error is returned and the lock may still not have taken: power-cycle the chip. A write never programs EEPROM by accident. With the unlock bit set, every write to a programmable register is stored in EEPROM as a power-on default (7.5.1.2, p. 18). A restart of the host during programming, or a lock that did not take, leaves the chip so. EnsureInitialized() therefore reads EEPROM_UL before its first register write; when EUN reads 1 it writes EUN = 0 and reads it back, and when it cannot confirm the lock it returns EepromVerifyFailed and has written nothing else ( A21 ). Outside ProgramPowerOnDefaults() and ProgramUserWord() no call programs an EEPROM word, except in the two residual risks of A21: switch-off row U5, and one bit flipped on the bus in the first EEPROM_UL reply. No write follows reset evidence. When the driver sees that the chip restarted (the setting bits of Configuration differ from its copy, EEPROM_Busy is set unexpectedly, or a result of 8000h follows a real one), the call returns UnexpectedReset , the driver is uninitialised, and no further write is sent until EnsureInitialized() has run again, except the switch-off, which follows its decision table . A reset to exactly the values the driver wrote is invisible ( A9 ), and so is a reset that changes only the limits or the offset ( residual risks ). 8000h is never a temperature. It reads as NoMeasurement before the first conversion and as UnexpectedReset after one. Switch-off always sends, except to a driver that never reached the chip (N1), to a chip that reads unlocked or busy, to a chip that answers nothing (U2), or to another device. Deinitialize() and SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) run one routine whose rules are the decision table below. An initialised driver always sends the one Configuration write with MOD = 01, whatever doubt it holds: a write in doubt is settled first by SetMode() , and when the settle read fails the shutdown write is sent anyway; when the settle finds reset evidence the lost-track rows apply. A driver that lost track of the chip (uninitialised after a failed programming, a reset or a start-up) reads EEPROM_UL first and never writes after a clean reply with EEPROM_Busy set: the chip is in its power-up load, which ignores writes, or programming a word, which forbids them (7.5.1.1 and 7.5.1.2, p. 18). It waits 7 ms and reads again, twice at most per call, and returns Timeout with nothing sent when the chip is still busy. It then writes the EEPROM lock (EUN = 0, a write that programs no EEPROM) and reads it back. Only the read that follows the last lock write decides: when it is clean and shows EUN = 1 the call returns EepromVerifyFailed and sends nothing, because the write would be programmed as the power-on default ( A21 ); a failed or garbled read is no evidence and the shutdown write goes out. A chip that answers neither the read nor the lock write gets nothing more ( Bus ). After a Device_ID mismatch the driver reads Device_ID once more and sends nothing when another part answers ( DeviceIdMismatch ). A failed write is not forgotten. The driver keeps its copy of the chip's configuration only for what the chip accepted; a write that failed is read back before the next change and the copy follows the chip. The alert flags are not lost. The three flags the chip clears on a read of Configuration are latched by every read the driver makes ( GetLatchedStatus() ). Every port failure propagates as Error::Bus ; no getter returns a stale or zero value after a failed read. Every wait is bounded: the power-up load by Config::reset_timeout_ms , an EEPROM word by Config::eeprom_timeout_ms , a one-shot by (n + 1) x 17.5 ms for n averaged conversions, WaitDataReady() by its argument (at most 20 s). The switch-off of a driver that lost track of the chip makes at most 8 transfers (9 after a Device_ID mismatch) and waits at most 14 ms (two 7 ms waits for a busy EEPROM), whatever the bus returns; SetMode() adds the settle reads (at most 5) in front. Deadlines are poll counts, not a clock: a port whose failed transfer itself takes long (an SMBus timeout of 25 ms to 35 ms) stretches a call by that time per poll. Config{} equals the datasheet reset values, proved by static_assert . A missing DelayUs() is a compile error; a missing ReadAlertPin() gives Error::Unsupported from ReadAlertPin() ; a missing Log() logs nothing. A misdeclared hook is a compile error. Deinitialize() that returns Ok leaves the chip in shutdown, its lowest-current state, except row N1 (the driver never reached the chip, so nothing is sent: a chip that converts from its power-on defaults keeps converting) and the residual risks (a reset the driver cannot see, row U5). A boot path that needs the chip in shutdown after a warm reset calls EnsureInitialized() first, then Deinitialize() or SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) . The bus-wide general-call reset is sent only with Config::allow_general_call . The SMBus alert response is not supported and sends nothing. Switch-off decision table ¶ The specification of Deinitialize() and SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) ; the code follows it row by row ( switchOff() and lockBeforeSwitchOff() in src/tmp117.ipp ), and each row has a test in tests/test_switch_off.cpp named after it. An EEPROM_UL reply is clean when bits 13:0 read 0 (Table 7-10, p. 30); a failed read and a reply with any of those bits set are no evidence . A clean reply is busy when EEPROM_Busy (bit 14) reads 1, whatever EUN reads. R is a read of EEPROM_UL, L the lock write (EEPROM_UL = 0000h), S the Configuration write with MOD = 01, C a Configuration write of SetMode() (MOD = 01 from the copy), D a read of Device_ID. Row Driver First read R Then, per attempt (at most 2): L , then R Transfers sent Status N1 Never reached the chip not sent none Deinitialize() : Ok ; SetMode() : NotInitialized N2 Last Device_ID read was another part D first: another part's word D DeviceIdMismatch , nothing else sent I1 Initialised, SetMode() not sent settle reads (any result), C the write's status; the copy follows the chip I2 Initialised, Deinitialize() not sent S the write's status; uninitialised afterwards I3 Initialised, SetMode() , the settle finds reset evidence as the U and W rows settle reads, then a U row as that U row U1 Lost track clean, EUN = 0, not busy R S the write's status U2 Lost track failed first L not acknowledged: stop R L Bus U3 Lost track EUN = 1, failed or no evidence an R after an L reads clean EUN = 0, not busy: stop R (L R){1,2} S the write's status U4 Lost track EUN = 1, failed or no evidence the R after the last L reads clean EUN = 1, not busy R L R L R EepromVerifyFailed , nothing else sent U5 Lost track EUN = 1, failed or no evidence the R after the last L failed or is no evidence R L R L R S the write's status, a warning logged U6 Lost track busy after two waits or an R after an L busy after the second wait R R R , or ending in R Timeout , nothing else sent; call again W1 Lost track, chip in its power-up load clean, busy, EUN = 0 any R busy the same way the busy R , then 7 ms, R again as the row the next R leads to W2 Lost track, a word being programmed clean, busy, EUN = 1 any R busy the same way the busy R , then 7 ms, R again as the row the next R leads to R1 Lost track after a reset command that failed but took effect clean, busy (the load) as W1 as W1 No write follows a clean busy R . The two 7 ms waits ( kEepromProgramUs , the typical programming time of 6.6, p. 7, and over four times the 1.5 ms load of A1) are a budget for the whole call, as in Figure 7-7 (p. 19: wait, then read EEPROM_Busy again). The datasheet prints no maximum; a chip still busy after 14 ms gets nothing (U6), and the caller calls again. A failed or garbled read is not busy: it is no evidence, as everywhere in the table. Evidence never carries over: a clean EUN = 1 seen before a lock write says nothing about that write (U5 after an earlier clean EUN = 1 still sends). The lock is written whatever the first read returned, except in U1, W1 and U6. U2 counts the R read just before the first L : after a busy reply and its wait, a failed R and a NACKed L also stop (three transfers: R R L ). N2 needs another part's word on that D : a failed read, DID 117h, or 0000h or FFFFh (the words of a line stuck at 0 or 1, which may still pass writes) go on by the other rows. Without a mismatch there is no D . R1: a soft or general-call reset whose ACK was lost ( SoftReset() , GeneralCallReset() , the relock of ProgramPowerOnDefaults() and ProgramUserWord() ) leaves the driver uninitialised and the chip in its load; the first R shows the load and W1 applies. U5 is the residual risk of A21: when every lock write was lost or did not take and no read-back succeeded, the shutdown word is programmed as a power-on default, and it is sent blind: a chip busy at that moment ignores it. Start-up never takes that risk: a lock not confirmed by a clean EUN = 0 refuses there, a garbled read included. The S of the lost-track rows carries the driver's copy of every field, not only MOD (FC-12): after a reset the alert polarity, alert function, averaging and cycle time of the copy replace the chip's EEPROM defaults. Harmless in shutdown; a board whose ALERT level comes only from programmed defaults sees the copy's polarity. Tests: N1, N2 (twice), I1, I2, I3, U1 to U6, W1 (twice), W2, R1 ("Switch-off row ..."), U3 also for a NACKed first lock write, U4 also after a failed first read-back, U5 also for every read failing and for the residual risk; a sweep fails every subset of the first eight transfers of the call on a locked, an unlocked, an unlockable, a programming and a loading chip, and checks the rows, the 8-transfer and 14 ms bounds, the busy rule, the effect ( Ok after a confirmed lock leaves the chip in shutdown) and the programming rule. The fuzz target checks the frames of U2 to U6 and N2 with no exclusion, the busy rule, and the effect: a switch-off that returns Ok leaves the model in shutdown outside the residual risks below: a write of the call lost or NACKed, a reply altered in the call, an initialised switch-off whose write the chip ignored although no read of the call showed EEPROM_Busy, and U5 ( tests/fuzz/fuzz_tmp117.cpp ). A read that shows EEPROM_Busy, in a settle or anywhere else, is reset evidence and is never excluded: the I3 tests "a settle read that shows EEPROM_Busy is reset evidence" (PROBE-R5-1) and "a lost ACK, a power cycle, then SetMode(Shutdown)" (D-2) and the corpus input regress-settle-reads-eeprom-busy pin it. Shutdown path states ¶ What the driver knows before the call, what it does, and where it ends. "Lost track" is IsInitialized() false after a start-up reached the chip. State before Event in the call Next state Chip afterwards Never started Deinitialize() or SetMode(Shutdown) Never started untouched Initialised SetMode(Shutdown) , write acknowledged Initialised, copy in shutdown shutdown Initialised SetMode(Shutdown) , write failed Initialised, write in doubt (settled by the next call) unknown Initialised SetMode(Shutdown) , the settle finds reset evidence (I3) Lost track, then as the U rows as the U rows Initialised Deinitialize() Lost track shutdown if the write was acknowledged Lost track lock confirmed or not read back (U1, U3, U5) Lost track shutdown if the write was acknowledged Lost track EUN reads 1 after the last lock write (U4) Lost track unchanged, unlocked: power-cycle it Lost track no answer (U2) Lost track unchanged; the next call starts again from the first read Lost track EEPROM_UL still busy after 14 ms (U6) Lost track unchanged; call again Any, after a Device_ID mismatch another part answers Device_ID (N2) Lost track that device untouched Lost track EnsureInitialized() succeeds Initialised as configured, lock confirmed Residual risks ¶ The owner's rule: an event so improbable that no reasonable design defends against it is documented here, not engineered. Each entry names the finding it comes from and, where one exists, the test that pins it. One flipped EUN bit in the first EEPROM_UL reply (R4-3, FC-9, F-A3, B-5). It needs a chip left unlocked by an interrupted programming and a bus error that turns exactly bit 15 of exactly that reply from 1 to 0 (or a line that goes stuck at 0 on that read) with bits 13:0 still clean. The bus has no CRC, so the driver takes it for a lock: start-up programs one limit word and then fails its read-back ( BadReply ); switch-off row U1 programs the shutdown word as a power-on default. At most one EEPROM word ("regress-r4-3"). A reset the driver cannot see, within the 1.5 ms load before an initialised switch-off or setter (FC-10, F-A1). A chip-only brown-out, another master's general call, or another driver object's GeneralCallReset() on the same bus. Rows I1 (no write in doubt) and I2 send with no read first, so the write lands in the load and is ignored, and a setter's write is lost the same way; the call returns Ok (or Bus under the NACK reading of A14). The next call that reads Configuration sees the reset ( UnexpectedReset ). The same holds for any state in which the chip ignores writes and that no read of the session has shown, such as an EEPROM still busy that an earlier corrupted reply hid. Start-up and the relock write the lock after the busy deadline (FC-11). tryLock() waits for EEPROM_Busy up to Config::eeprom_timeout_ms and then writes EUN = 0 whatever it reads. Only a chip still programming after that deadline (50 ms by default, about seven times the typical time) gets a write while busy; that chip is faulty, the call already reports Timeout or EepromVerifyFailed , and the lock write programs nothing. The lost-track shutdown word carries the copy (FC-12). See the decision table notes. A reset that changes only the limits or the offset (F-A5). Reset evidence is read from Configuration, EEPROM_Busy and 8000h. When the EEPROM holds the driver's Configuration word but other limits or another offset, a reset outside the first conversion passes ReadStatus() and CheckHealth() ; see A9 . An offset below about -200 °C (F-A8). It saturates a cold result to 8000h, which reads as NoMeasurement or UnexpectedReset ( A7 ); no real use needs it. Corruption the bus cannot reveal (B-6). A write whose data is corrupted on the way (no CRC), a read reply that repeats the previous transfer, and a legitimate 8000h caused by offset saturation. A part swapped, or an address clash, after a good start-up (D-1). A Device_ID mismatch seen by a read ( ReadTemperatureRaw(Verify::Device) , a status poll) returns DeviceIdMismatch , but only CheckHealth() uninitialises the driver; the setters and ProgramUserWord() that follow still write to whatever answers at the address, and ProgramUserWord() can program one word of it before its final identity read fails. It needs a part exchanged or a second device appearing on a running bus; the switch-off (N2) never writes to another part. After a DeviceIdMismatch , call Deinitialize() and EnsureInitialized() before any other call. Rows W1, W2, R1 and U6 rest on one truthful EEPROM_UL reply (D-3). One reply that reads 0000h (a stuck-0 line) or has bit 14 flipped, at the moment the chip is loading or programming, reads as "clean, EUN = 0, not busy": row U1 sends the shutdown write into the load or into a programming word, where it is ignored or forbidden. A second reset between the last read and that write, and a reset no read has shown before an initialised switch-off or setter, are the same class as the one above (FC-10). Whole-call failure of every read while the chip loads is row U5. Stale one-shot result under the alternative reading of A12 (D-4). If a Configuration read in therm mode does not clear Data_Ready, a Data_Ready left by an earlier continuous conversion that nobody read can complete a one-shot at once: ReadOneShotMilliC() returns the previous result with Ok while the new conversion still runs. The chip ends in shutdown on its own, so no switch-off is affected; read Temp_Result once (or call ReadTemperatureMilliC() ) before starting a one-shot in therm mode if the board's chip reads that way ( A12 ). Row U5, a write sent blind. No clean read-back of the last lock write: the shutdown word is sent, programmed when the lock did not take ( A21 ), and ignored by a chip that is busy at that moment. Depends on ¶ Dependency Version Why A C++20 compiler GCC 10, Clang 13 or later Concepts constrain the port CMake 3.16 or later Generates tmp117_version.h Your port The bus, 5 kHz to 400 kHz, with a repeated START and address 0 for one byte; the delay; optionally the ALERT pin and logging ( Porting ) Nothing else: no RTOS, no SDK, no other repository of the org. Threading ¶ The driver is not thread-safe and takes no lock. Use each driver object from one task at a time, or guard every call on it with one mutex; the layer that owns the driver owns that lock, and the bus lock when several chips share a bus. Nothing may run in an ISR: every call can block for a bus transfer or a delay. Separate objects share no state. Errors ¶ tmp117::Error inside tmp117::Result<T> . Values 0 to 9 are the shared base set; this driver returns every one of them except Crc and DeviceFault , because the TMP117's bus has no checksum and the chip reports no sensing fault. Values from 16 are specific to this chip. Error Value Returned when Ok 0 The call succeeded NotInitialized 1 EnsureInitialized() has not succeeded, a reset was seen, or Deinitialize() ran since InvalidArgument 2 A Config field or argument is out of range ( Validate() ); nothing was sent Bus 3 A port hook returned false Timeout 4 The power-up load, a conversion, WaitDataReady() or an EEPROM word did not finish in time; a switch-off found the EEPROM still busy after 14 ms (nothing sent) DeviceIdMismatch 5 Device_ID is not 0x117 in bits 11:0; a switch-off found another part (nothing sent) Crc 6 Never returned (no CRC on this chip) Busy 7 A one-shot is pending DeviceFault 8 Never returned (the chip reports no sensing fault) Unsupported 9 ReadAlertPin() without the hook, GeneralCallReset() without the opt-in, SmbusAlertResponse() UnexpectedReset 16 Reset evidence: the chip restarted behind the driver's back. The driver is uninitialised afterwards NoMeasurement 17 Temp_Result reads 8000h and no result has been seen since the start EepromVerifyFailed 18 The EEPROM readback differs from what was written, or the chip could not be locked again BadReply 19 A bit that must read 0 reads 1, or a register does not read back what was written The API guide says what to do about each. Memory ¶ No heap, no exceptions, no RTTI, no std::function , no std::string , no printf and no static mutable state. A driver object holds the bus reference, the address, two Config copies, a few flags and the transfer buffers (a 3-byte write and a 2-byte read): about 100 bytes (104 with the mock port). No stack buffer is larger than 8 bytes (the register words of a programming call); the setters copy a Config (32 bytes) on the stack. Platform ¶ Platform-free: the same code runs on any target with a C++20 compiler, including the host tests. The ESP-IDF port in examples/esp32 is an example, not part of the driver. Deviations from the standard ¶ None.

A chip that answers neither the read nor the lock write gets nothing more ( Bus ). After a Device_ID mismatch the driver reads Device_ID once more and sends nothing when another part answers ( DeviceIdMismatch ). A failed write is not forgotten. The driver keeps its copy of the chip's configuration only for what the chip accepted; a write that failed is read back before the next change and the copy follows the chip. The alert flags are not lost. The three flags the chip clears on a read of Configuration are latched by every read the driver makes ( GetLatchedStatus() ). Every port failure propagates as Error::Bus ; no getter returns a stale or zero value after a failed read. Every wait is bounded: the power-up load by Config::reset_timeout_ms , an EEPROM word by Config::eeprom_timeout_ms , a one-shot by (n + 1) x 17.5 ms for n averaged conversions, WaitDataReady() by its argument (at most 20 s). The switch-off of a driver that lost track of the chip makes at most 8 transfers (9 after a Device_ID mismatch) and waits at most 14 ms (two 7 ms waits for a busy EEPROM), whatever the bus returns; SetMode() adds the settle reads (at most 5) in front. Deadlines are poll counts, not a clock: a port whose failed transfer itself takes long (an SMBus timeout of 25 ms to 35 ms) stretches a call by that time per poll. Config{} equals the datasheet reset values, proved by static_assert . A missing DelayUs() is a compile error; a missing ReadAlertPin() gives Error::Unsupported from ReadAlertPin() ; a missing Log() logs nothing. A misdeclared hook is a compile error. Deinitialize() that returns Ok leaves the chip in shutdown, its lowest-current state, except row N1 (the driver never reached the chip, so nothing is sent: a chip that converts from its power-on defaults keeps converting) and the residual risks (a reset the driver cannot see, row U5). A boot path that needs the chip in shutdown after a warm reset calls EnsureInitialized() first, then Deinitialize() or SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) . The bus-wide general-call reset is sent only with Config::allow_general_call . The SMBus alert response is not supported and sends nothing.
docs.title: Promises

docs.text: The specification of Deinitialize() and SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) ; the code follows it row by row ( switchOff() and lockBeforeSwitchOff() in src/tmp117.ipp ), and each row has a test in tests/test_switch_off.cpp named after it. An EEPROM_UL reply is clean when bits 13:0 read 0 (Table 7-10, p. 30); a failed read and a reply with any of those bits set are no evidence . A clean reply is busy when EEPROM_Busy (bit 14) reads 1, whatever EUN reads. R is a read of EEPROM_UL, L the lock write (EEPROM_UL = 0000h), S the Configuration write with MOD = 01, C a Configuration write of SetMode() (MOD = 01 from the copy), D a read of Device_ID. Row Driver First read R Then, per attempt (at most 2): L , then R Transfers sent Status N1 Never reached the chip not sent none Deinitialize() : Ok ; SetMode() : NotInitialized N2 Last Device_ID read was another part D first: another part's word D DeviceIdMismatch , nothing else sent I1 Initialised, SetMode() not sent settle reads (any result), C the write's status; the copy follows the chip I2 Initialised, Deinitialize() not sent S the write's status; uninitialised afterwards I3 Initialised, SetMode() , the settle finds reset evidence as the U and W rows settle reads, then a U row as that U row U1 Lost track clean, EUN = 0, not busy R S the write's status U2 Lost track failed first L not acknowledged: stop R L Bus U3 Lost track EUN = 1, failed or no evidence an R after an L reads clean EUN = 0, not busy: stop R (L R){1,2} S the write's status U4 Lost track EUN = 1, failed or no evidence the R after the last L reads clean EUN = 1, not busy R L R L R EepromVerifyFailed , nothing else sent U5 Lost track EUN = 1, failed or no evidence the R after the last L failed or is no evidence R L R L R S the write's status, a warning logged U6 Lost track busy after two waits or an R after an L busy after the second wait R R R , or ending in R Timeout , nothing else sent; call again W1 Lost track, chip in its power-up load clean, busy, EUN = 0 any R busy the same way the busy R , then 7 ms, R again as the row the next R leads to W2 Lost track, a word being programmed clean, busy, EUN = 1 any R busy the same way the busy R , then 7 ms, R again as the row the next R leads to R1 Lost track after a reset command that failed but took effect clean, busy (the load) as W1 as W1 No write follows a clean busy R . The two 7 ms waits ( kEepromProgramUs , the typical programming time of 6.6, p. 7, and over four times the 1.5 ms load of A1) are a budget for the whole call, as in Figure 7-7 (p. 19: wait, then read EEPROM_Busy again). The datasheet prints no maximum; a chip still busy after 14 ms gets nothing (U6), and the caller calls again. A failed or garbled read is not busy: it is no evidence, as everywhere in the table. Evidence never carries over: a clean EUN = 1 seen before a lock write says nothing about that write (U5 after an earlier clean EUN = 1 still sends). The lock is written whatever the first read returned, except in U1, W1 and U6. U2 counts the R read just before the first L : after a busy reply and its wait, a failed R and a NACKed L also stop (three transfers: R R L ). N2 needs another part's word on that D : a failed read, DID 117h, or 0000h or FFFFh (the words of a line stuck at 0 or 1, which may still pass writes) go on by the other rows. Without a mismatch there is no D . R1: a soft or general-call reset whose ACK was lost ( SoftReset() , GeneralCallReset() , the relock of ProgramPowerOnDefaults() and ProgramUserWord() ) leaves the driver uninitialised and the chip in its load; the first R shows the load and W1 applies. U5 is the residual risk of A21: when every lock write was lost or did not take and no read-back succeeded, the shutdown word is programmed as a power-on default, and it is sent blind: a chip busy at that moment ignores it. Start-up never takes that risk: a lock not confirmed by a clean EUN = 0 refuses there, a garbled read included. The S of the lost-track rows carries the driver's copy of every field, not only MOD (FC-12): after a reset the alert polarity, alert function, averaging and cycle time of the copy replace the chip's EEPROM defaults. Harmless in shutdown; a board whose ALERT level comes only from programmed defaults sees the copy's polarity. Tests: N1, N2 (twice), I1, I2, I3, U1 to U6, W1 (twice), W2, R1 ("Switch-off row ..."), U3 also for a NACKed first lock write, U4 also after a failed first read-back, U5 also for every read failing and for the residual risk; a sweep fails every subset of the first eight transfers of the call on a locked, an unlocked, an unlockable, a programming and a loading chip, and checks the rows, the 8-transfer and 14 ms bounds, the busy rule, the effect ( Ok after a confirmed lock leaves the chip in shutdown) and the programming rule. The fuzz target checks the frames of U2 to U6 and N2 with no exclusion, the busy rule, and the effect: a switch-off that returns Ok leaves the model in shutdown outside the residual risks below: a write of the call lost or NACKed, a reply altered in the call, an initialised switch-off whose write the chip ignored although no read of the call showed EEPROM_Busy, and U5 ( tests/fuzz/fuzz_tmp117.cpp ). A read that shows EEPROM_Busy, in a settle or anywhere else, is reset evidence and is never excluded: the I3 tests "a settle read that shows EEPROM_Busy is reset evidence" (PROBE-R5-1) and "a lost ACK, a power cycle, then SetMode(Shutdown)" (D-2) and the corpus input regress-settle-reads-eeprom-busy pin it.

docs.text: The owner's rule: an event so improbable that no reasonable design defends against it is documented here, not engineered. Each entry names the finding it comes from and, where one exists, the test that pins it. One flipped EUN bit in the first EEPROM_UL reply (R4-3, FC-9, F-A3, B-5). It needs a chip left unlocked by an interrupted programming and a bus error that turns exactly bit 15 of exactly that reply from 1 to 0 (or a line that goes stuck at 0 on that read) with bits 13:0 still clean. The bus has no CRC, so the driver takes it for a lock: start-up programs one limit word and then fails its read-back ( BadReply ); switch-off row U1 programs the shutdown word as a power-on default. At most one EEPROM word ("regress-r4-3"). A reset the driver cannot see, within the 1.5 ms load before an initialised switch-off or setter (FC-10, F-A1). A chip-only brown-out, another master's general call, or another driver object's GeneralCallReset() on the same bus. Rows I1 (no write in doubt) and I2 send with no read first, so the write lands in the load and is ignored, and a setter's write is lost the same way; the call returns Ok (or Bus under the NACK reading of A14). The next call that reads Configuration sees the reset ( UnexpectedReset ). The same holds for any state in which the chip ignores writes and that no read of the session has shown, such as an EEPROM still busy that an earlier corrupted reply hid. Start-up and the relock write the lock after the busy deadline (FC-11). tryLock() waits for EEPROM_Busy up to Config::eeprom_timeout_ms and then writes EUN = 0 whatever it reads. Only a chip still programming after that deadline (50 ms by default, about seven times the typical time) gets a write while busy; that chip is faulty, the call already reports Timeout or EepromVerifyFailed , and the lock write programs nothing. The lost-track shutdown word carries the copy (FC-12). See the decision table notes. A reset that changes only the limits or the offset (F-A5). Reset evidence is read from Configuration, EEPROM_Busy and 8000h. When the EEPROM holds the driver's Configuration word but other limits or another offset, a reset outside the first conversion passes ReadStatus() and CheckHealth() ; see A9 . An offset below about -200 °C (F-A8). It saturates a cold result to 8000h, which reads as NoMeasurement or UnexpectedReset ( A7 ); no real use needs it. Corruption the bus cannot reveal (B-6). A write whose data is corrupted on the way (no CRC), a read reply that repeats the previous transfer, and a legitimate 8000h caused by offset saturation. A part swapped, or an address clash, after a good start-up (D-1). A Device_ID mismatch seen by a read ( ReadTemperatureRaw(Verify::Device) , a status poll) returns DeviceIdMismatch , but only CheckHealth() uninitialises the driver; the setters and ProgramUserWord() that follow still write to whatever answers at the address, and ProgramUserWord() can program one word of it before its final identity read fails. It needs a part exchanged or a second device appearing on a running bus; the switch-off (N2) never writes to another part. After a DeviceIdMismatch , call Deinitialize() and EnsureInitialized() before any other call. Rows W1, W2, R1 and U6 rest on one truthful EEPROM_UL reply (D-3). One reply that reads 0000h (a stuck-0 line) or has bit 14 flipped, at the moment the chip is loading or programming, reads as "clean, EUN = 0, not busy": row U1 sends the shutdown write into the load or into a programming word, where it is ignored or forbidden. A second reset between the last read and that write, and a reset no read has shown before an initialised switch-off or setter, are the same class as the one above (FC-10). Whole-call failure of every read while the chip loads is row U5. Stale one-shot result under the alternative reading of A12 (D-4). If a Configuration read in therm mode does not clear Data_Ready, a Data_Ready left by an earlier continuous conversion that nobody read can complete a one-shot at once: ReadOneShotMilliC() returns the previous result with Ok while the new conversion still runs. The chip ends in shutdown on its own, so no switch-off is affected; read Temp_Result once (or call ReadTemperatureMilliC() ) before starting a one-shot in therm mode if the board's chip reads that way ( A12 ). Row U5, a write sent blind. No clean read-back of the last lock write: the shutdown word is sent, programmed when the lock did not take ( A21 ), and ignored by a chip that is busy at that moment.

docs.text: The driver is not thread-safe and takes no lock. Use each driver object from one task at a time, or guard every call on it with one mutex; the layer that owns the driver owns that lock, and the bus lock when several chips share a bus. Nothing may run in an ISR: every call can block for a bus transfer or a delay. Separate objects share no state.

docs.text: tmp117::Error inside tmp117::Result<T> . Values 0 to 9 are the shared base set; this driver returns every one of them except Crc and DeviceFault , because the TMP117's bus has no checksum and the chip reports no sensing fault. Values from 16 are specific to this chip. Error Value Returned when Ok 0 The call succeeded NotInitialized 1 EnsureInitialized() has not succeeded, a reset was seen, or Deinitialize() ran since InvalidArgument 2 A Config field or argument is out of range ( Validate() ); nothing was sent Bus 3 A port hook returned false Timeout 4 The power-up load, a conversion, WaitDataReady() or an EEPROM word did not finish in time; a switch-off found the EEPROM still busy after 14 ms (nothing sent) DeviceIdMismatch 5 Device_ID is not 0x117 in bits 11:0; a switch-off found another part (nothing sent) Crc 6 Never returned (no CRC on this chip) Busy 7 A one-shot is pending DeviceFault 8 Never returned (the chip reports no sensing fault) Unsupported 9 ReadAlertPin() without the hook, GeneralCallReset() without the opt-in, SmbusAlertResponse() UnexpectedReset 16 Reset evidence: the chip restarted behind the driver's back. The driver is uninitialised afterwards NoMeasurement 17 Temp_Result reads 8000h and no result has been seen since the start EepromVerifyFailed 18 The EEPROM readback differs from what was written, or the chip could not be locked again BadReply 19 A bit that must read 0 reads 1, or a register does not read back what was written The API guide says what to do about each.
docs.title: Errors

docs.text: No heap, no exceptions, no RTTI, no std::function , no std::string , no printf and no static mutable state. A driver object holds the bus reference, the address, two Config copies, a few flags and the transfer buffers (a 3-byte write and a 2-byte read): about 100 bytes (104 with the mock port). No stack buffer is larger than 8 bytes (the register words of a programming call); the setters copy a Config (32 bytes) on the stack.

docs.text: Examples ¶ One folder per platform under examples/ , each with its own port, built by CI on every pull request. The driver itself has no platform code; Platforms lists what exists. Host ¶ examples/host/ runs the driver on any PC against a simulated TMP117, through the host port host_tmp117_port.hpp . No hardware: cmake -S examples/host -B build-example && cmake --build build-example && ./build-example/tmp117_host_example The host tests build it with warnings as errors and run it (CTest tmp117_host_example ). ESP32 ¶ ESP-IDF applications that run the driver on an ESP32-C6 DevKitC-1; the wiring is in the example folder's README and the port in esp32_tmp117_port.hpp . The project points EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS at the repository root, which is the driver's ESP-IDF component. The apps ¶ App What it shows Source CI tmp117_basic_example Start the TMP117 from menuconfig values and log the temperature twice a second tmp117_basic_example.cpp yes Build and flash one (from examples/esp32 , ESP-IDF environment loaded): ./scripts/build_app.sh tmp117_basic_example Release ./scripts/flash_app.sh flash_monitor tmp117_basic_example Release Source of this table: examples/esp32/app_config.yml . Set up once ¶ git submodule update --init examples/esp32/scripts # the ESP-IDF build scripts cd examples/esp32 . $IDF_PATH /export.sh # ESP-IDF v5.5 ./scripts/build_app.sh list # every app and build type The scripts read app_config.yml (the same file this page's table comes from) and build each app as its own firmware image. Pads sit centred on each side at the stated pitch; the datasheet's land pattern is the reference for a board. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . WSON-6, 6 pins and an exposed pad (5 Pin Configuration and Functions, p. 4 ). Pin Name Type (domain) Function Driver hook If unused Datasheet 1 SCL bus (V+) Serial clock, 5 kHz to 400 kHz (A15) Write() / WriteRead() - 5, p. 4 2 GND ground Ground - - 5, p. 4 3 ALERT open drain (V+) Over-temperature alert or data-ready, open drain, needs a pull-up ReadAlertPin(bool&) Leave open 5, p. 4 4 ADD0 digital in (V+) Address select: GND 0x48, V+ 0x49, SDA 0x4A, SCL 0x4B - - 7.5.3.1.2, p. 21 5 V+ power (V+) Supply, 1.8 V to 5.5 V - - 6.3, p. 5 6 SDA bus (V+) Serial data, open drain, needs a pull-up Write() / WriteRead() - 5, p. 4 EP Thermal pad 1 not connected (GND) Thermal pad, left unconnected - - 8.2, p. 33 Source of this table and of the chip figures: docs/hardware.yml . The DSBGA balls are A1 SDA, A2 SCL, B1 V+, B2 GND, C1 ADD0 and C2 ALERT. The thermal pad of the WSON is left unconnected; the datasheet's layout page (section 10) is the place to check that for your board. ALERT and the driver's own reads. In alert mode a read of Configuration clears HIGH_Alert and LOW_Alert and so releases the ALERT pin (7.4.4.1, p. 16). The driver reads Configuration in ReadStatus() , WaitDataReady() , StartOneShot() , CheckHealth() and the settle after a failed write, so an application that services ALERT as a level interrupt can find the pin released by that polling. The flags are kept in GetLatchedStatus() ; see the API guide . Not hardware-verified. Arrows between blocks carry signals or data in the direction they point (both ways where they have two heads). The package pins stand on the left and right edges with their numbers, each wired to the block it reaches. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . The temperature sensor is an internal bipolar transistor and an ADC. The control logic and its oscillator run the conversion cycle, the register bank holds the settings and the result, and the EEPROM supplies the register values at power-up. The serial interface is I2C and SMBus compatible. Typical connections ¶ TMP117: Typical connections Figure description and sources A schematic. The MCU is on the left, each of its pins level with the chip pin it connects to; above each wire is the hook of the driver's port that drives or reads it. Supply pins point up to their supply and decoupling, ground pins down. Pins on the right carry the loads and the pins tied to a supply or ground; a cross marks a pin left open. A dot is a junction; wires that cross without a dot are not connected. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . Part Kind Value Connects Datasheet U2 MCU - VDD: +3V3, GND: GND, SCL: SCL, SDA: SDA, IRQ: ALERT 8.2, p. 33 C1 capacitor 0.1 µF +3V3, GND 8.2, p. 33 R1 resistor 5 kΩ +3V3, SDA 8.2, p. 33 R2 resistor 5 kΩ +3V3, ALERT 8.2, p. 33 Export a circuit for a schematic or PCB tool: kokeb-docs hardware --kicad-netlist OUT.net --circuit typical . Both pull-ups are 5 kΩ in the datasheet's figure and can be higher or lower. SCL needs a pull-up only if the MCU pin is open drain. Use a ceramic bypass capacitor rated for the whole temperature range and place it close to V+. Do not heat the chip with its own supply current: the datasheet's section 8.2.2.2 gives the self-heating, which matters when averaging is high and the cycle is short. Bus settings ¶ Setting Value Clock 5 kHz to 400 kHz (fast mode). The datasheet lists 1 kHz, but a 3-byte write then outlasts the 20 ms minimum bus timeout ( A15 ) Address 7-bit, 0x48 to 0x4B from ADD0: GND 0x48 , V+ 0x49 , SDA 0x4A , SCL 0x4B ; pass it to the constructor Write START, address + W, pointer, high byte, low byte, STOP Read START, address + W, pointer, repeated START, address + R, high byte, low byte, STOP Words Every register is 16 bits, high byte first; the pointer byte has its upper four bits at 0 Pointer The driver sends the pointer with every read, so it never relies on the chip remembering it TMP117: I2C register word Figure description and sources One I2C register word of the TMP117, 24 bits in a row from the most significant (left, sent first) to the least significant (right). Each row is one kind of frame; each coloured box a field, with its first and last bit number under it. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . One register read on the I2C bus Figure description and sources Two participants, the host and the TMP117. The host sends START, address 0x48 with the write bit and the pointer byte 0x00, Temp_Result. It repeats START with address 0x48 and the read bit. The chip returns the high byte and the low byte of the register. The host answers the last byte with NACK and ends the transaction with STOP. Drawn from: docs/model/bus-frame.seq.yml . The waveform under these frames is on On the bus . The driver also uses two special transfers: the general-call reset (address 0x00 , byte 06h , only with allow_general_call ) and, in a later release, the SMBus alert response. Power ¶ Mode Supply current (typical) Where Shutdown 0.15 µA (0.5 µA maximum at 25 °C) 6.5, p. 6 Standby between conversions 1.25 µA 6.5, p. 6 One result per second, no averaging 3.5 µA 6.5, p. 6 One result per second, 8 averaged 16 µA 6.5, p. 6 Converting 135 µA 6.5, p. 6 Deinitialize() puts a chip it has reached in shutdown; on a driver that never reached the chip it sends nothing (row N1 of the decision table ). The supply is 1.8 V to 5.5 V over the whole temperature range, and 1.7 V up to 70 °C (6.3, p. 5). docs.text: Installation ¶ Add the driver to a CMake project on any MCU or on your PC, or to an ESP-IDF project. It is a header-only C++20 library with no dependencies, and one root CMakeLists.txt serves every build. Requirements ¶ A C++20 compiler: GCC 10+, Clang 13+ or a current MSVC. The driver uses concepts and requires . CMake 3.16 or later: it generates the version header the driver includes ( tmp117_version.h ). No RTOS, heap, exceptions or RTTI: every call is noexcept and returns a Result . Get the source ¶ A git submodule keeps the driver pinned to the version you chose: git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-tmp117.git external/driver-tmp117 git submodule update --init external/driver-tmp117 Only inc/ , src/ , cmake/ , _config/ and CMakeLists.txt are needed to build. The examples are not; the ESP32 example even has its own submodule ( examples/esp32/scripts ). CMake (any MCU, any host) ¶ This is the MCU-neutral path: the same two lines work for a host build, STM32 (CubeMX CMake projects), RP2040 (Pico SDK), nRF (nRF Connect SDK) or any other CMake toolchain. Platforms lists what has a port today. add_subdirectory ( external/driver-tmp117 ) target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE tmp117::tmp117 ) tmp117::tmp117 is an alias of the tmp117 INTERFACE target. It carries the include directories (the headers and the generated version header) and requires C++20, so your target does not need to set either. Option Default Effect TMP117_ENABLE_WARNINGS OFF -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic on every target that links the driver TMP117_BUILD_TESTS OFF Builds the host tests in tests/ and the host example ( Testing and CI ) Installed package ¶ To use the driver without adding its source tree to your build, install it and find the package: cmake -S external/driver-tmp117 -B build-tmp117 cmake --install build-tmp117 --prefix /opt/sdk find_package ( tmp117 0.1 REQUIRED ) # with CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/sdk target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE tmp117::tmp117 ) The target is tmp117::tmp117 in both cases ( EXPORT_NAME ), so a project can switch between add_subdirectory() and find_package() without changing its target_link_libraries() . The headers and the generated tmp117_version.h go to include/tmp117/inc/ , the template implementation to include/tmp117/src/tmp117.ipp . The host CI installs the package and builds a consumer against it on every pull request ( Testing and CI ). ESP-IDF ¶ Under ESP-IDF the root CMakeLists.txt registers the repository itself as a component: with ESP_PLATFORM set it calls idf_component_register() from the same build settings, with the menu in _config/Kconfig . There is no wrapper to copy. ESP-IDF names a component after its folder, so the name in your REQUIRES is the name of the folder the repository is in. Pick one of these: How What to write Component name Folder of extra components list(APPEND EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS external/driver-tmp117) in the project CMakeLists.txt , before project.cmake driver-tmp117 (the folder) Submodule under components/ git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-tmp117.git components/tmp117 tmp117 (the folder) Component manager, from git The dependency below in main/idf_component.yml tmp117 (the key) # main/idf_component.yml of your project dependencies : tmp117 : git : https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-tmp117.git version : v0.1.0 # a release tag Your component then declares REQUIRES tmp117 (or the folder name), and idf.py menuconfig shows the driver's menu ( Configuration ). The ESP32 example uses the first way, with EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS pointing at the repository root, and works out the folder name in main/CMakeLists.txt ; CI builds it on every pull request. The repository has no idf_component.yml . The component manager does not need one for a git dependency; the manifest is only required to publish to the ESP Component Registry, which these releases do not use. If registry publishing is chosen, the manifest is added at the root then. How the build is organised ¶ Layer File Role Settings cmake/tmp117_build_settings.cmake Target name, include directories, sources, version: the single source of truth Library CMakeLists.txt INTERFACE target, alias, install rules and the package export, or the ESP-IDF component Tool configuration _config/ Doxyfile, the docs site, Kconfig, clang-format, clang-tidy and the linters Version ¶ The version is set once in the settings file and written into tmp117_version.h in the build tree at configure time. The Doxyfile ( _config/Doxyfile ) carries a copy; a host test fails when it differs. Read it at run time: const char * v = tmp117 :: GetDriverVersion (); // "0.1.0" Next ¶ Quickstart runs the driver on your PC, then on your MCU; Porting writes the port for your MCU.

docs.text: A git submodule keeps the driver pinned to the version you chose: git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-tmp117.git external/driver-tmp117 git submodule update --init external/driver-tmp117 Only inc/ , src/ , cmake/ , _config/ and CMakeLists.txt are needed to build. The examples are not; the ESP32 example even has its own submodule ( examples/esp32/scripts ).
docs.title: Get the source

docs.text: This is the MCU-neutral path: the same two lines work for a host build, STM32 (CubeMX CMake projects), RP2040 (Pico SDK), nRF (nRF Connect SDK) or any other CMake toolchain. Platforms lists what has a port today. add_subdirectory ( external/driver-tmp117 ) target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE tmp117::tmp117 ) tmp117::tmp117 is an alias of the tmp117 INTERFACE target. It carries the include directories (the headers and the generated version header) and requires C++20, so your target does not need to set either. Option Default Effect TMP117_ENABLE_WARNINGS OFF -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic on every target that links the driver TMP117_BUILD_TESTS OFF Builds the host tests in tests/ and the host example ( Testing and CI )
docs.title: CMake (any MCU, any host)

docs.text: To use the driver without adding its source tree to your build, install it and find the package: cmake -S external/driver-tmp117 -B build-tmp117 cmake --install build-tmp117 --prefix /opt/sdk find_package ( tmp117 0.1 REQUIRED ) # with CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/sdk target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE tmp117::tmp117 ) The target is tmp117::tmp117 in both cases ( EXPORT_NAME ), so a project can switch between add_subdirectory() and find_package() without changing its target_link_libraries() . The headers and the generated tmp117_version.h go to include/tmp117/inc/ , the template implementation to include/tmp117/src/tmp117.ipp . The host CI installs the package and builds a consumer against it on every pull request ( Testing and CI ).
docs.title: Installed package

docs.text: Under ESP-IDF the root CMakeLists.txt registers the repository itself as a component: with ESP_PLATFORM set it calls idf_component_register() from the same build settings, with the menu in _config/Kconfig . There is no wrapper to copy. ESP-IDF names a component after its folder, so the name in your REQUIRES is the name of the folder the repository is in. Pick one of these: How What to write Component name Folder of extra components list(APPEND EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS external/driver-tmp117) in the project CMakeLists.txt , before project.cmake driver-tmp117 (the folder) Submodule under components/ git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-tmp117.git components/tmp117 tmp117 (the folder) Component manager, from git The dependency below in main/idf_component.yml tmp117 (the key) # main/idf_component.yml of your project dependencies : tmp117 : git : https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-tmp117.git version : v0.1.0 # a release tag Your component then declares REQUIRES tmp117 (or the folder name), and idf.py menuconfig shows the driver's menu ( Configuration ). The ESP32 example uses the first way, with EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS pointing at the repository root, and works out the folder name in main/CMakeLists.txt ; CI builds it on every pull request. The repository has no idf_component.yml . The component manager does not need one for a git dependency; the manifest is only required to publish to the ESP Component Registry, which these releases do not use. If registry publishing is chosen, the manifest is added at the root then.
docs.title: ESP-IDF

docs.text: The version is set once in the settings file and written into tmp117_version.h in the build tree at configure time. The Doxyfile ( _config/Doxyfile ) carries a copy; a host test fails when it differs. Read it at run time: const char * v = tmp117 :: GetDriverVersion (); // "0.1.0"

docs.text: Language standard ¶ The driver declares the C++ standard it needs once, in the language: block of driver.yml . Everything else that names the standard (the CMake files, the compiler flags, .clang-format , the workflows, the README badge and the sentences that say "a C++20 compiler") repeats that declaration, and tools/check_language.py keeps them equal. language : standard : 20 # the minimum ISO C++ standard: a consumer needs at least this profile : KB-CPP20 # the handbook profile of that standard profile_version : "1.0" # the handbook release that defines it misra : "MISRA C++:2023" # the MISRA edition the driver is analysed against compilers : # the oldest versions the driver promises to build with (quote them) gcc : "10" clang : "13" tested : [ 20 ] # every standard CI compiles the headers under; includes the minimum effective_from : 2026-11-15 # the date this declaration took effect What is checked ¶ python3 -I tools/check_language.py (part of the preflight and the repository checks) fails when the block is missing a key, has an unknown one, or names a profile that is not KB-CPP<standard> ; tested does not include standard , or names a standard below it; cxx_std_N or CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD in a CMake file, Standard: in .clang-format , or a __cplusplus assertion names another standard, or the library target never requires the declared one; a -std=c++N flag or a workflow std input names a standard that is not in tested ; the README badge, "a C++20 compiler", or "GCC 10+" and "Clang 13+" differ from the block. A driver.yml without the block is a note, so a driver that has not taken the template yet still passes; python3 tools/scaffold.py --check-drift --fix adds the block. Whether the profile is known, current, supported or retired is not decided here but by the organisation's registry, which kokeb-labs/ci-tools keeps ( tools/standards/standards.yml , checked by tools/standards/check_standards.py ). Raising the standard ¶ Raising standard is a breaking change for everyone who builds with an older compiler (a minor release before 1.0, a major release after). Change the block, run python3 -I tools/check_language.py --fix to rewrite every site, read the diff (prose about the profile's own rules is left alone on purpose), then run the preflight. The full playbook (profile differences, feature gates, a multi-standard CI matrix, the review items, the MISRA edition) is kept with the registry in kokeb-labs/ci-tools, docs/language-standards.md .
