docs.text: Testing and CI ¶ How the driver is checked: host tests against a model of the chip, a fuzzer that corrupts what the chip sends back, compiled documentation, an install test, ESP32 and Cortex-M builds, static analysis and measured quality gates, on every pull request. Host tests ¶ The tests build the real driver against a register model of the TMP117 written from the datasheet alone: the register map and reset values, the power-up load and EEPROM programming with a virtual clock, the clear-on-read flags, Table 7-7, the one-shot return to shutdown, the 8000h value, and the unlock and relock of the EEPROM. They also inject faults: bus errors, a wrong Device_ID, a reset at any transfer, a stuck conversion, a stuck EEPROM, lines stuck at zeros, ones or the last word, one flipped reply at call k, and a write that was applied but reported as failed. They build with the firmware's flags, -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti , and warnings as errors, on GCC and Clang. cmake -S . -B build -DTMP117_BUILD_TESTS = ON cmake --build build ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure File Covers tests/test_tmp117.cpp Lifecycle, identity, power-up, golden frames, measurement, one-shot, flag latch, ALERT pin, setters, doubt and settle, reset evidence, resets, optional hooks tests/test_eeprom.cpp The programming sequence, the relock on every failure path (a NACK at each write), timeouts, the traceability words, the readings of ambiguities A2, A5 and A6 tests/test_faults.cpp Stuck lines, a flipped reply, a reset injected at every transfer of a script, no write after reset evidence, every ambiguity reading through a whole session tests/test_safety_regressions.cpp Switch-off after a failed settle, start-up on an unlocked EEPROM, a one-shot under both readings of A19, a raw read during a one-shot, a line stuck at 0 on the status and identity reads, switch-off of an uninitialised driver whose reads fail, the switch-off force flag, a reserved EEPROM_UL bit, the one-shot doubt cleared by a write tests/test_switch_off.cpp One test per row of the switch-off decision table , a sweep over every pattern of failed transfers of the call, and the third review round's probes ( regress-r3-* ) tests/test_bus_faults.cpp Every transfer of every operation failing in turn is reported as Bus tests/fuzz/ The fuzz target; CTest replays its corpus ( tmp117_fuzz_tmp117_corpus ), see below tests/test_errors.cpp The base Error values are 0 to 9; every chip-specific value (16 and up) is returned by some call tests/test_version.cpp The version getters follow the generated header (also against a 9.8.7 probe) tests/test_kconfig.cpp KconfigDefaults() with and without CONFIG_ values tests/compile_fail/ Code that must not compile, each for its EXPECT: diagnostic: a port without DelayUs() , a void ReadAlertPin() , a DelayUs(uint16_t) , a hook with a narrowed parameter or without noexcept , an invalid CheckedConfig , a class that is not a port tests/mock_tmp117.hpp The register model, with its own register map; the bus framing is in mock_tmp117_bus.hpp tests/test_model.cpp The model's register map, reset values, Table 7-7 and Table 7-1 against the driver's, with static_assert ; the model's own behaviour tests/test_support.hpp A driver on a mock port ( Rig ) and the helpers the tests share tests/check_version_copy.cmake _config/Doxyfile carries the CMake version examples/host/ The host example, built with the test flags and run ( tmp117_host_example ) tests/check_install.cmake Installs into a scratch prefix and builds tests/install_consumer/ with find_package(tmp117) tests/check_doxygen.cmake Doxygen with _config/Doxyfile and warnings as errors, when doxygen is installed The model stands alone ¶ tests/mock_tmp117.hpp is written from the datasheet, not from the driver: it does not include tmp117_registers.hpp or tmp117_types.hpp . Its register map, field masks, reset values, cycle-time table and timing are its own (namespace tmp117_test::chip , each with the datasheet section), so a wrong constant in the driver cannot hide behind the same wrong constant in the model (handbook KB-TST-030). tests/test_model.cpp compares the two at compile time: // Register map (Table 7-3, p. 25). static_assert (( chip :: kTempResult == reg :: kTempResult ) && ( chip :: kConfiguration == reg :: kConfiguration ) && ( chip :: kHighLimit == reg :: kHighLimit ) && ( chip :: kLowLimit == reg :: kLowLimit ) && ( chip :: kEepromUl == reg :: kEepromUnlock ) && ( chip :: kEeprom1 == reg :: kEeprom1 ) && ( chip :: kEeprom2 == reg :: kEeprom2 ) && ( chip :: kTempOffset == reg :: kTempOffset ) && ( chip :: kEeprom3 == reg :: kEeprom3 ) && ( chip :: kDeviceId == reg :: kDeviceId )); // Configuration fields (Table 7-6, p. 27-28) and EEPROM unlock (Table 7-10, p. 30). static_assert (( chip :: kHighAlert == reg :: kCfgHighAlert ) && ( chip :: kLowAlert == reg :: kCfgLowAlert ) && ( chip :: kDataReady == reg :: kCfgDataReady ) && ( chip :: kEepromBusy == reg :: kCfgEepromBusy ) && ( chip :: kTherm == reg :: kCfgTherm ) && ( chip :: kPol == reg :: kCfgPolarity ) && ( chip :: kDrAlert == reg :: kCfgDrAlert ) && ( chip :: kSoftReset == reg :: kCfgSoftReset )); static_assert (( chip :: kModMask == reg :: CfgMod :: kMask ) && ( chip :: kConvMask == reg :: CfgConv :: kMask ) && ( chip :: kAvgMask == reg :: CfgAvg :: kMask ) && ( chip :: kWritable == reg :: kCfgWritableMask ) && ( chip :: kEepromStored == reg :: kCfgEepromMask )); static_assert (( chip :: kEun == reg :: kUnlockEun ) && ( chip :: kUlBusy == reg :: kUnlockBusy )); // Reset values and identity (Table 7-3; section 7.6.11). static_assert (( chip :: kConfigurationReset == reg :: kConfigurationReset ) && ( chip :: kHighLimitReset == reg :: kHighLimitReset ) && ( chip :: kLowLimitReset == reg :: kLowLimitReset ) && ( chip :: kTempResultReset == reg :: kTempResultReset ) && ( chip :: kDeviceIdValue == reg :: kDeviceIdValue )); // Timing: the driver waits at least what the chip needs (section 6.5, 6.6, Table 7-6). static_assert (( chip :: kPowerOnUs == tmp117 :: kPowerOnLoadUs ) && ( chip :: kSoftResetUs == tmp117 :: kSoftResetUs ) && ( chip :: kConversionMaxUs == tmp117 :: kConversionMaxUs ) && ( chip :: kProgramTypUs == tmp117 :: kEepromProgramUs )); // Bus (section 7.5.3.1.2 and 7.5.3.1.6). static_assert (( chip :: kAddressGnd == tmp117 :: kI2cAddress ) && ( chip :: kGeneralCall == reg :: kGeneralCallAddress ) && ( chip :: kGeneralCallReset == reg :: kGeneralCallReset )); // The clear-on-read flags the driver latches are the three the model clears on a read. static_assert ( reg :: kCfgClearOnRead == ( uint32_t { chip :: kHighAlert } | uint32_t { chip :: kLowAlert } | uint32_t { chip :: kDataReady })); When the build stops on one of these, one of the two maps is wrong: check it against the section the model names, and fix that one. A new register goes into both, with its check. Every behaviour found on hardware becomes a fault mode of the model and a test that fails on the code before the fix; a chip with timing gets a virtual clock in the model (here Elapse() , driven by the mock port's DelayUs() ). Fuzz tests ¶ Everything the driver reads comes from the chip over the bus, so the data read is what a noisy cable, a wrong part or a broken chip controls. tests/fuzz/fuzz_tmp117.cpp lets libFuzzer choose a configuration, then up to 64 driver calls, and on every bus transfer what the bus does: pass it to the model, fail it, flip bits of the data read or replace it, lose an acknowledged write, or store a write and lose its acknowledge. Between calls it can change the chip: a wrong Device_ID, a power cycle the driver was not told about, a stuck conversion or EEPROM, any temperature. After every call it checks the driver's promises and aborts, naming the line, when one breaks: a failed call returns an Error the enum defines and T{} ; a temperature is inside the range of the 16-bit result; before EnsureInitialized() has reached the chip no call makes a transfer ( Deinitialize() returns Ok , row N1), afterwards, once the driver is uninitialised, only Deinitialize() and SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) do, and InvalidArgument means nothing was sent; UnexpectedReset leaves the driver uninitialised; the driver never writes Temp_Result, Device_ID, EEPROM1, EEPROM3 or a pointer outside the map, and never sends the general-call reset without the opt-in; SetMode(Shutdown) on an initialised driver always puts a Configuration write with MOD 01 on the bus, whatever the settle reads returned, unless it was refused for an unlocked EEPROM or another device (N2), or the settle found reset evidence (I3: the next rule applies); SetMode(Shutdown) and Deinitialize() of a driver that lost track of the chip put that write on the bus unless the EEPROM_UL reply the driver received after its last lock write was clean with EUN = 1 (row U4 of the decision table ), the read before the first lock write and that write both failed (U2), the EEPROM stayed busy (U6, Timeout ) or another device answered (N2). There is no exclusion for failed, garbled or altered reads; a U4 refusal with no altered reply in the call also needs the chip model's true EUN to be 1, and an N2 refusal a model Device_ID that is not 117h; in a switch-off call no write follows an EEPROM_UL reply received clean with EEPROM_Busy set (rows W1, W2, U6); the effect, not the frame: a switch-off that returns Ok leaves the chip model in shutdown, except in the residual risks : a write of the call lost or NACKed, a reply altered in the call, an initialised switch-off (no read first) whose write the chip ignored, and row U5 (no clean read-back of the last lock write); while no read reply was altered, no EEPROM word is programmed outside ProgramPowerOnDefaults() and ProgramUserWord() , except by a switch-off whose last lock write was not read back clean (U5, the residual risk of A21); every log line is a non-empty plain-text message. When the model becomes your chip's, keep the target and turn its checks into your chip's promises: every value range the datasheet defines, and every state the driver must never reach. # libFuzzer needs Clang (on macOS, Homebrew's LLVM) cmake -S . -B build-fuzz -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER = clang++ -DTMP117_BUILD_TESTS = ON -DTMP117_BUILD_FUZZERS = ON cmake --build build-fuzz --target fuzz_tmp117 ./build-fuzz/tests/fuzz/fuzz_tmp117 -max_total_time = 120 tests/fuzz/corpus/fuzz_tmp117 The same file also builds without libFuzzer as fuzz_replay_fuzz_tmp117 , and CTest replays every input in tests/fuzz/corpus/fuzz_tmp117/ on GCC and Clang ( tmp117_fuzz_tmp117_corpus ): the seeds ( seed-* , start-* ), and every input that ever broke a promise ( regress-* , fourteen today), so a fixed bug stays fixed. CI fuzzes for 120 s on every pull request, from the seeds plus a corpus it keeps between runs (job Host quality / fuzz ). Quality gates ¶ The Host quality job measures the library code, inc/ and src/ only (tests and examples are left out), and fails when a value is over the limits of this repository's assurance level, high (set in .kokeb/handbook.yml , defined by the handbook's ADR-0020): Gate Tool and how it is measured Limit at high Complexity lizard 1.24.1, modified cyclomatic complexity ( -m : a switch counts once) per function CCN at most 15 Function length lizard, lines of code per function at most 60 Parameters lizard, per function at most 6 Line coverage GCC 14 --coverage -O0 , every CTest, gcovr 8.7 --merge-lines (a template's lines count once across its instances), --exclude-unreachable-branches --exclude-throw-branches at least 85 % Branch coverage same run at least 75 % MC/DC GCC -fcondition-coverage , same run measured, not gated at high (100 % at safety ) Sanitizers Clang, -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all , every CTest no report Fuzzing libFuzzer with ASan and UBSan, 120 s per target no broken promise The reports are in the run's host-quality-reports artifact and its step summary. To run the gates locally: # Coverage (GCC 14 or later), then the complexity limits cmake -S . -B build-cov -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER = g++-14 -DTMP117_BUILD_TESTS = ON \ -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS = "--coverage -O0 -fcondition-coverage" cmake --build build-cov && ctest --test-dir build-cov gcovr --root . --filter inc/ --filter src/ --merge-lines --exclude-unreachable-branches --txt build-cov lizard -m -C 15 -L 60 -a 6 inc src # Sanitizers (Clang) cmake -S . -B build-san -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER = clang++ -DTMP117_BUILD_TESTS = ON \ -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS = "-fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all -O1 -g" cmake --build build-san && ctest --test-dir build-san --output-on-failure The fuzz gate runs locally as shown in Fuzz tests . clang-tidy 20 ( _config/.clang-tidy : bugprone, CERT, clang-analyzer, cppcoreguidelines, modernize, performance, portability and readability, each disabled check with its reason) and cppcheck (strict) run in the C++ lint and Repository checks jobs and fail on any finding. The MISRA job ( ci-misra.yml ) runs the shared ru-misra workflow of ci-tools at level high : it traces a host build and the Cortex-M build ( tmp117_optimised_build ) of every translation unit, checks them against MISRA C++:2023 and the handbook's C++20 profile (the CodeQL coding-standards and profile packs, plus the validated clang-tidy and cppcheck checks), and reports each finding against the handbook's compliance matrix and deviation records. A finding is fixed in the code; a deliberate exception names its deviation on the line before it ( // codeql::misra_deviation_next_line(MD-CPP-009) above the .ipp include of inc/tmp117.hpp ). Until the repository is public the job runs with open_source_prerelease: true , the declaration that the code is released under the licence in LICENSE and is to be published. The MISRA scan, rehearsed locally ¶ The scan runs only in CI, and a first push has paid for the same few findings again and again. tools/misra_lint.py (standard-library Python, no build) catches those classes before the push; tools/preflight.sh runs it as the misra-lint step, which cannot be skipped, and its --selftest as misra-lint-selftest . It reads the C++ files ( *.hpp , *.cpp , *.ipp ) of inc/ , src/ , tests/ and examples/ and prints file:line Rule N.N.N message : Rule Reported Severity 9.4.1 an if ... else if chain that does not end in a plain else (at the last else if ) error 7.0.3 arithmetic, comparison or conversion on a char : c - '0' , c >= '0' , token[0] == '-' , static_cast<char>(byte) error 0.1.2 a call statement that drops the result of a function the tree declares with a class return type error (scalar result: warning) 13.3.3 a function whose declaration and definition use different parameter names error KB-CPP-012 an include in inc/ or src/ outside the driver's library subset error 8.0.1 an operand of a logical and / or that is a comparison or bitwise expression and is not parenthesised warning Severity. An error fails the preflight; a warning is printed and counted in the summary line ( misra_lint: N file(s), E error(s), W warning(s) ) and does not. A finding is an error only when its rule is one the CI scan blocks on and it is in inc/ or src/ ; every finding in tests/ or examples/ is a warning, as are 8.0.1 everywhere and --void-casts ( (void)expr; , which the scan accepts). --strict turns every warning into an error, for a reviewer who wants the whole list. This split is derived from CI evidence, not from the rule text: the scan reported 7.0.3, 9.4.1, 0.1.2 and 13.3.3 as failure and 8.0.1 as warning , only failure annotations fail the job, all findings listed were in inc/ and src/ , and drivers whose CI is green still carry else if chains in tests/ . Revisit it if CodeQL is ever seen blocking on a finding in tests/ or examples/ , or on 8.0.1: move that rule or folder into the error set ( TRACED and the severities in tools/misra_lint.py ). The check is a token scan without types: it reports what it can decide and stays silent otherwise, so a clean run does not replace the scan, but an error is an error. Fix the code: compare characters through a table or std::array<char, 1> equality, convert a byte with static_cast<char> , end the chain in else , give the declaration and the definition the same parameter names, use the returned value or discard it with static_cast<void> . A deliberate exception carries the deviation the scan reads ( // codeql::misra_deviation_next_line(MD-CPP-...) on the line before) or // misra-lint: ignore 8.0.1 on the line. --strict-precedence ( a < b + 1 ) reports more 8.0.1. Evaluation order in checks, rehearsed locally ¶ The arguments of a call are evaluated in an unspecified order. GCC on x86-64 reads them right to left; Clang and GCC on aarch64 read them left to right, so a call such as Check(d.Write(v), was_up, sent()) reads sent() before the write on the x86-64 CI runner only: a "nothing was sent" promise passes vacuously, and a positive one aborts on a correct driver. No local rehearsal on Apple silicon or in the aarch64 container sees it. Compute the result first ( const auto r = d.Write(v); Check(r, was_up, sent()); ), or pass the probe and read it inside the helper after the call. tools/eval_order_check.py (standard-library Python, run as python3 -I ) reports a call whose arguments hold a driver operation ( d.Op(...) ) and, in another argument, a read of a probe ( sent() , Transfers() , pending() , ++ ), or whose arguments read the fuzzer's input twice ( in.Byte() , FuzzConfig(in) : the same corpus file then decodes into different calls per compiler). tools/preflight.sh runs it over tests/ and examples/ as the eval-order step (its --selftest as eval-order-selftest ); neither can be skipped. It prints file:line: error eval-order: <call> and exits 1 on a finding; // eval-order: ignore on the line of the call is the deliberate exception. It is a token scan without types: it reports what it can decide, and a clean run does not replace review. Where a fuzz target has a positive check on a counter, keep a one-edit mutant of the counter that must abort the corpus replay (see tests/fuzz/CMakeLists.txt of a driver that has one), so the check cannot become vacuous unseen. The include subset is read from handbook_check.py of a ci-tools checkout ( CI_TOOLS_DIR , default ../ci-tools ), so the two never differ; without the checkout the built-in list of ADR-0017 applies. The preflight also runs that handbook_check.py itself (the handbook-check step; skipped, with the reason named, only when the checkout or PyYAML is missing), lints tests/install_consumer/main.cpp with clang-tidy like every other C++ file (it is built by its own CMake project, so it is not in the host build's compilation database), and checks the first-push gitlink: after git add -A , examples/esp32/scripts must be a gitlink (mode 160000). Documentation snippets ¶ Every C++ block on this site is included from tests/docs/ , which the host build compiles (target tmp117_doc_snippets ) with the driver instantiated over the documented port. A change to the API that breaks a page breaks the build first. The README's example is a generated copy of the same file; kokeb-docs check fails when it drifts. CI workflows ¶ Everything runs from ci.yml , which calls one workflow file per check and ends in the CI gate job, the single required check ( CI gate / gate ). Job What it checks Host tests GCC, then Clang (one job), build and run every test above, then build and run examples/host on its own Host quality The gates above: complexity, coverage, sanitizers, fuzzing Cross-compile arm-none-eabi-g++ for Cortex-M0+, M4F and M7F with the strict flags, warnings as errors (nothing linked) C++ lint clang-format and clang-tidy over the sources MISRA MISRA C++:2023 and the C++20 profile on traced host and Cortex-M builds, at level high (see Quality gates ) Docs Strict site build ( _config/mkdocs.yml ), figure and generated-region drift, Doxygen ( _config/Doxyfile ), offline link check, Lighthouse Repository checks One job: DCO on pull requests, the org standard, Markdown and YAML lint, the Kokeb Labs handbook rules for .kokeb/handbook.yml (by rule ID), template drift (warns only) and cppcheck over the driver sources; a second job runs the handbook's source checks (include guards, bus requirements, raw access) CI gate Passes only if every job above passed: the one required check The ESP32 examples job builds every app in examples/esp32/app_config.yml , for each listed ESP-IDF version and build type, with the repository root as the driver's component, and lints the example sources. The gate needs it too. The workflows call the shared, versioned workflows of kokeb-labs/ci-tools at @v1 . On hardware ¶ The tests prove the driver against a model of the chip written from the datasheet; a bench proves the model. The driver states how far it has been checked as a level, in driver.yml ( hardware.level ) and as the README badge: Level Means H0 Host model only: never run on a chip. Releases say not hardware-verified H1 A defined bench rig ran the example; the rig document and the logs are kept H2 A hardware engineer reviewed the rig and the steps and signed off An MCU example ( Examples ) is the bench test: it logs the temperature twice a second. Warm the chip and watch the value rise. Record the rig and the result in the pull request's bench-status section; the hardware-validation skill says what evidence each level needs and how to write the rig document. tools/check_hardware.py keeps the level, the badge and the evidence in step.

docs.text: The tests build the real driver against a register model of the TMP117 written from the datasheet alone: the register map and reset values, the power-up load and EEPROM programming with a virtual clock, the clear-on-read flags, Table 7-7, the one-shot return to shutdown, the 8000h value, and the unlock and relock of the EEPROM. They also inject faults: bus errors, a wrong Device_ID, a reset at any transfer, a stuck conversion, a stuck EEPROM, lines stuck at zeros, ones or the last word, one flipped reply at call k, and a write that was applied but reported as failed. They build with the firmware's flags, -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti , and warnings as errors, on GCC and Clang. cmake -S . -B build -DTMP117_BUILD_TESTS = ON cmake --build build ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure File Covers tests/test_tmp117.cpp Lifecycle, identity, power-up, golden frames, measurement, one-shot, flag latch, ALERT pin, setters, doubt and settle, reset evidence, resets, optional hooks tests/test_eeprom.cpp The programming sequence, the relock on every failure path (a NACK at each write), timeouts, the traceability words, the readings of ambiguities A2, A5 and A6 tests/test_faults.cpp Stuck lines, a flipped reply, a reset injected at every transfer of a script, no write after reset evidence, every ambiguity reading through a whole session tests/test_safety_regressions.cpp Switch-off after a failed settle, start-up on an unlocked EEPROM, a one-shot under both readings of A19, a raw read during a one-shot, a line stuck at 0 on the status and identity reads, switch-off of an uninitialised driver whose reads fail, the switch-off force flag, a reserved EEPROM_UL bit, the one-shot doubt cleared by a write tests/test_switch_off.cpp One test per row of the switch-off decision table , a sweep over every pattern of failed transfers of the call, and the third review round's probes ( regress-r3-* ) tests/test_bus_faults.cpp Every transfer of every operation failing in turn is reported as Bus tests/fuzz/ The fuzz target; CTest replays its corpus ( tmp117_fuzz_tmp117_corpus ), see below tests/test_errors.cpp The base Error values are 0 to 9; every chip-specific value (16 and up) is returned by some call tests/test_version.cpp The version getters follow the generated header (also against a 9.8.7 probe) tests/test_kconfig.cpp KconfigDefaults() with and without CONFIG_ values tests/compile_fail/ Code that must not compile, each for its EXPECT: diagnostic: a port without DelayUs() , a void ReadAlertPin() , a DelayUs(uint16_t) , a hook with a narrowed parameter or without noexcept , an invalid CheckedConfig , a class that is not a port tests/mock_tmp117.hpp The register model, with its own register map; the bus framing is in mock_tmp117_bus.hpp tests/test_model.cpp The model's register map, reset values, Table 7-7 and Table 7-1 against the driver's, with static_assert ; the model's own behaviour tests/test_support.hpp A driver on a mock port ( Rig ) and the helpers the tests share tests/check_version_copy.cmake _config/Doxyfile carries the CMake version examples/host/ The host example, built with the test flags and run ( tmp117_host_example ) tests/check_install.cmake Installs into a scratch prefix and builds tests/install_consumer/ with find_package(tmp117) tests/check_doxygen.cmake Doxygen with _config/Doxyfile and warnings as errors, when doxygen is installed
docs.title: Host tests

docs.text: tests/mock_tmp117.hpp is written from the datasheet, not from the driver: it does not include tmp117_registers.hpp or tmp117_types.hpp . Its register map, field masks, reset values, cycle-time table and timing are its own (namespace tmp117_test::chip , each with the datasheet section), so a wrong constant in the driver cannot hide behind the same wrong constant in the model (handbook KB-TST-030). tests/test_model.cpp compares the two at compile time: // Register map (Table 7-3, p. 25). static_assert (( chip :: kTempResult == reg :: kTempResult ) && ( chip :: kConfiguration == reg :: kConfiguration ) && ( chip :: kHighLimit == reg :: kHighLimit ) && ( chip :: kLowLimit == reg :: kLowLimit ) && ( chip :: kEepromUl == reg :: kEepromUnlock ) && ( chip :: kEeprom1 == reg :: kEeprom1 ) && ( chip :: kEeprom2 == reg :: kEeprom2 ) && ( chip :: kTempOffset == reg :: kTempOffset ) && ( chip :: kEeprom3 == reg :: kEeprom3 ) && ( chip :: kDeviceId == reg :: kDeviceId )); // Configuration fields (Table 7-6, p. 27-28) and EEPROM unlock (Table 7-10, p. 30). static_assert (( chip :: kHighAlert == reg :: kCfgHighAlert ) && ( chip :: kLowAlert == reg :: kCfgLowAlert ) && ( chip :: kDataReady == reg :: kCfgDataReady ) && ( chip :: kEepromBusy == reg :: kCfgEepromBusy ) && ( chip :: kTherm == reg :: kCfgTherm ) && ( chip :: kPol == reg :: kCfgPolarity ) && ( chip :: kDrAlert == reg :: kCfgDrAlert ) && ( chip :: kSoftReset == reg :: kCfgSoftReset )); static_assert (( chip :: kModMask == reg :: CfgMod :: kMask ) && ( chip :: kConvMask == reg :: CfgConv :: kMask ) && ( chip :: kAvgMask == reg :: CfgAvg :: kMask ) && ( chip :: kWritable == reg :: kCfgWritableMask ) && ( chip :: kEepromStored == reg :: kCfgEepromMask )); static_assert (( chip :: kEun == reg :: kUnlockEun ) && ( chip :: kUlBusy == reg :: kUnlockBusy )); // Reset values and identity (Table 7-3; section 7.6.11). static_assert (( chip :: kConfigurationReset == reg :: kConfigurationReset ) && ( chip :: kHighLimitReset == reg :: kHighLimitReset ) && ( chip :: kLowLimitReset == reg :: kLowLimitReset ) && ( chip :: kTempResultReset == reg :: kTempResultReset ) && ( chip :: kDeviceIdValue == reg :: kDeviceIdValue )); // Timing: the driver waits at least what the chip needs (section 6.5, 6.6, Table 7-6). static_assert (( chip :: kPowerOnUs == tmp117 :: kPowerOnLoadUs ) && ( chip :: kSoftResetUs == tmp117 :: kSoftResetUs ) && ( chip :: kConversionMaxUs == tmp117 :: kConversionMaxUs ) && ( chip :: kProgramTypUs == tmp117 :: kEepromProgramUs )); // Bus (section 7.5.3.1.2 and 7.5.3.1.6). static_assert (( chip :: kAddressGnd == tmp117 :: kI2cAddress ) && ( chip :: kGeneralCall == reg :: kGeneralCallAddress ) && ( chip :: kGeneralCallReset == reg :: kGeneralCallReset )); // The clear-on-read flags the driver latches are the three the model clears on a read. static_assert ( reg :: kCfgClearOnRead == ( uint32_t { chip :: kHighAlert } | uint32_t { chip :: kLowAlert } | uint32_t { chip :: kDataReady })); When the build stops on one of these, one of the two maps is wrong: check it against the section the model names, and fix that one. A new register goes into both, with its check. Every behaviour found on hardware becomes a fault mode of the model and a test that fails on the code before the fix; a chip with timing gets a virtual clock in the model (here Elapse() , driven by the mock port's DelayUs() ).
docs.title: The model stands alone

docs.text: Everything the driver reads comes from the chip over the bus, so the data read is what a noisy cable, a wrong part or a broken chip controls. tests/fuzz/fuzz_tmp117.cpp lets libFuzzer choose a configuration, then up to 64 driver calls, and on every bus transfer what the bus does: pass it to the model, fail it, flip bits of the data read or replace it, lose an acknowledged write, or store a write and lose its acknowledge. Between calls it can change the chip: a wrong Device_ID, a power cycle the driver was not told about, a stuck conversion or EEPROM, any temperature. After every call it checks the driver's promises and aborts, naming the line, when one breaks: a failed call returns an Error the enum defines and T{} ; a temperature is inside the range of the 16-bit result; before EnsureInitialized() has reached the chip no call makes a transfer ( Deinitialize() returns Ok , row N1), afterwards, once the driver is uninitialised, only Deinitialize() and SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) do, and InvalidArgument means nothing was sent; UnexpectedReset leaves the driver uninitialised; the driver never writes Temp_Result, Device_ID, EEPROM1, EEPROM3 or a pointer outside the map, and never sends the general-call reset without the opt-in; SetMode(Shutdown) on an initialised driver always puts a Configuration write with MOD 01 on the bus, whatever the settle reads returned, unless it was refused for an unlocked EEPROM or another device (N2), or the settle found reset evidence (I3: the next rule applies); SetMode(Shutdown) and Deinitialize() of a driver that lost track of the chip put that write on the bus unless the EEPROM_UL reply the driver received after its last lock write was clean with EUN = 1 (row U4 of the decision table ), the read before the first lock write and that write both failed (U2), the EEPROM stayed busy (U6, Timeout ) or another device answered (N2). There is no exclusion for failed, garbled or altered reads; a U4 refusal with no altered reply in the call also needs the chip model's true EUN to be 1, and an N2 refusal a model Device_ID that is not 117h; in a switch-off call no write follows an EEPROM_UL reply received clean with EEPROM_Busy set (rows W1, W2, U6); the effect, not the frame: a switch-off that returns Ok leaves the chip model in shutdown, except in the residual risks : a write of the call lost or NACKed, a reply altered in the call, an initialised switch-off (no read first) whose write the chip ignored, and row U5 (no clean read-back of the last lock write); while no read reply was altered, no EEPROM word is programmed outside ProgramPowerOnDefaults() and ProgramUserWord() , except by a switch-off whose last lock write was not read back clean (U5, the residual risk of A21); every log line is a non-empty plain-text message. When the model becomes your chip's, keep the target and turn its checks into your chip's promises: every value range the datasheet defines, and every state the driver must never reach. # libFuzzer needs Clang (on macOS, Homebrew's LLVM) cmake -S . -B build-fuzz -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER = clang++ -DTMP117_BUILD_TESTS = ON -DTMP117_BUILD_FUZZERS = ON cmake --build build-fuzz --target fuzz_tmp117 ./build-fuzz/tests/fuzz/fuzz_tmp117 -max_total_time = 120 tests/fuzz/corpus/fuzz_tmp117 The same file also builds without libFuzzer as fuzz_replay_fuzz_tmp117 , and CTest replays every input in tests/fuzz/corpus/fuzz_tmp117/ on GCC and Clang ( tmp117_fuzz_tmp117_corpus ): the seeds ( seed-* , start-* ), and every input that ever broke a promise ( regress-* , fourteen today), so a fixed bug stays fixed. CI fuzzes for 120 s on every pull request, from the seeds plus a corpus it keeps between runs (job Host quality / fuzz ).
docs.title: Fuzz tests

docs.text: The Host quality job measures the library code, inc/ and src/ only (tests and examples are left out), and fails when a value is over the limits of this repository's assurance level, high (set in .kokeb/handbook.yml , defined by the handbook's ADR-0020): Gate Tool and how it is measured Limit at high Complexity lizard 1.24.1, modified cyclomatic complexity ( -m : a switch counts once) per function CCN at most 15 Function length lizard, lines of code per function at most 60 Parameters lizard, per function at most 6 Line coverage GCC 14 --coverage -O0 , every CTest, gcovr 8.7 --merge-lines (a template's lines count once across its instances), --exclude-unreachable-branches --exclude-throw-branches at least 85 % Branch coverage same run at least 75 % MC/DC GCC -fcondition-coverage , same run measured, not gated at high (100 % at safety ) Sanitizers Clang, -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all , every CTest no report Fuzzing libFuzzer with ASan and UBSan, 120 s per target no broken promise The reports are in the run's host-quality-reports artifact and its step summary. To run the gates locally: # Coverage (GCC 14 or later), then the complexity limits cmake -S . -B build-cov -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER = g++-14 -DTMP117_BUILD_TESTS = ON \ -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS = "--coverage -O0 -fcondition-coverage" cmake --build build-cov && ctest --test-dir build-cov gcovr --root . --filter inc/ --filter src/ --merge-lines --exclude-unreachable-branches --txt build-cov lizard -m -C 15 -L 60 -a 6 inc src # Sanitizers (Clang) cmake -S . -B build-san -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER = clang++ -DTMP117_BUILD_TESTS = ON \ -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS = "-fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all -O1 -g" cmake --build build-san && ctest --test-dir build-san --output-on-failure The fuzz gate runs locally as shown in Fuzz tests . clang-tidy 20 ( _config/.clang-tidy : bugprone, CERT, clang-analyzer, cppcoreguidelines, modernize, performance, portability and readability, each disabled check with its reason) and cppcheck (strict) run in the C++ lint and Repository checks jobs and fail on any finding. The MISRA job ( ci-misra.yml ) runs the shared ru-misra workflow of ci-tools at level high : it traces a host build and the Cortex-M build ( tmp117_optimised_build ) of every translation unit, checks them against MISRA C++:2023 and the handbook's C++20 profile (the CodeQL coding-standards and profile packs, plus the validated clang-tidy and cppcheck checks), and reports each finding against the handbook's compliance matrix and deviation records. A finding is fixed in the code; a deliberate exception names its deviation on the line before it ( // codeql::misra_deviation_next_line(MD-CPP-009) above the .ipp include of inc/tmp117.hpp ). Until the repository is public the job runs with open_source_prerelease: true , the declaration that the code is released under the licence in LICENSE and is to be published.
docs.title: Quality gates

docs.text: The scan runs only in CI, and a first push has paid for the same few findings again and again. tools/misra_lint.py (standard-library Python, no build) catches those classes before the push; tools/preflight.sh runs it as the misra-lint step, which cannot be skipped, and its --selftest as misra-lint-selftest . It reads the C++ files ( *.hpp , *.cpp , *.ipp ) of inc/ , src/ , tests/ and examples/ and prints file:line Rule N.N.N message : Rule Reported Severity 9.4.1 an if ... else if chain that does not end in a plain else (at the last else if ) error 7.0.3 arithmetic, comparison or conversion on a char : c - '0' , c >= '0' , token[0] == '-' , static_cast<char>(byte) error 0.1.2 a call statement that drops the result of a function the tree declares with a class return type error (scalar result: warning) 13.3.3 a function whose declaration and definition use different parameter names error KB-CPP-012 an include in inc/ or src/ outside the driver's library subset error 8.0.1 an operand of a logical and / or that is a comparison or bitwise expression and is not parenthesised warning Severity. An error fails the preflight; a warning is printed and counted in the summary line ( misra_lint: N file(s), E error(s), W warning(s) ) and does not. A finding is an error only when its rule is one the CI scan blocks on and it is in inc/ or src/ ; every finding in tests/ or examples/ is a warning, as are 8.0.1 everywhere and --void-casts ( (void)expr; , which the scan accepts). --strict turns every warning into an error, for a reviewer who wants the whole list. This split is derived from CI evidence, not from the rule text: the scan reported 7.0.3, 9.4.1, 0.1.2 and 13.3.3 as failure and 8.0.1 as warning , only failure annotations fail the job, all findings listed were in inc/ and src/ , and drivers whose CI is green still carry else if chains in tests/ . Revisit it if CodeQL is ever seen blocking on a finding in tests/ or examples/ , or on 8.0.1: move that rule or folder into the error set ( TRACED and the severities in tools/misra_lint.py ). The check is a token scan without types: it reports what it can decide and stays silent otherwise, so a clean run does not replace the scan, but an error is an error. Fix the code: compare characters through a table or std::array<char, 1> equality, convert a byte with static_cast<char> , end the chain in else , give the declaration and the definition the same parameter names, use the returned value or discard it with static_cast<void> . A deliberate exception carries the deviation the scan reads ( // codeql::misra_deviation_next_line(MD-CPP-...) on the line before) or // misra-lint: ignore 8.0.1 on the line. --strict-precedence ( a < b + 1 ) reports more 8.0.1.
docs.title: The MISRA scan, rehearsed locally

docs.text: The arguments of a call are evaluated in an unspecified order. GCC on x86-64 reads them right to left; Clang and GCC on aarch64 read them left to right, so a call such as Check(d.Write(v), was_up, sent()) reads sent() before the write on the x86-64 CI runner only: a "nothing was sent" promise passes vacuously, and a positive one aborts on a correct driver. No local rehearsal on Apple silicon or in the aarch64 container sees it. Compute the result first ( const auto r = d.Write(v); Check(r, was_up, sent()); ), or pass the probe and read it inside the helper after the call. tools/eval_order_check.py (standard-library Python, run as python3 -I ) reports a call whose arguments hold a driver operation ( d.Op(...) ) and, in another argument, a read of a probe ( sent() , Transfers() , pending() , ++ ), or whose arguments read the fuzzer's input twice ( in.Byte() , FuzzConfig(in) : the same corpus file then decodes into different calls per compiler). tools/preflight.sh runs it over tests/ and examples/ as the eval-order step (its --selftest as eval-order-selftest ); neither can be skipped. It prints file:line: error eval-order: <call> and exits 1 on a finding; // eval-order: ignore on the line of the call is the deliberate exception. It is a token scan without types: it reports what it can decide, and a clean run does not replace review. Where a fuzz target has a positive check on a counter, keep a one-edit mutant of the counter that must abort the corpus replay (see tests/fuzz/CMakeLists.txt of a driver that has one), so the check cannot become vacuous unseen. The include subset is read from handbook_check.py of a ci-tools checkout ( CI_TOOLS_DIR , default ../ci-tools ), so the two never differ; without the checkout the built-in list of ADR-0017 applies. The preflight also runs that handbook_check.py itself (the handbook-check step; skipped, with the reason named, only when the checkout or PyYAML is missing), lints tests/install_consumer/main.cpp with clang-tidy like every other C++ file (it is built by its own CMake project, so it is not in the host build's compilation database), and checks the first-push gitlink: after git add -A , examples/esp32/scripts must be a gitlink (mode 160000).
docs.title: Evaluation order in checks, rehearsed locally

docs.text: Every C++ block on this site is included from tests/docs/ , which the host build compiles (target tmp117_doc_snippets ) with the driver instantiated over the documented port. A change to the API that breaks a page breaks the build first. The README's example is a generated copy of the same file; kokeb-docs check fails when it drifts.
docs.title: Documentation snippets

docs.text: Everything runs from ci.yml , which calls one workflow file per check and ends in the CI gate job, the single required check ( CI gate / gate ). Job What it checks Host tests GCC, then Clang (one job), build and run every test above, then build and run examples/host on its own Host quality The gates above: complexity, coverage, sanitizers, fuzzing Cross-compile arm-none-eabi-g++ for Cortex-M0+, M4F and M7F with the strict flags, warnings as errors (nothing linked) C++ lint clang-format and clang-tidy over the sources MISRA MISRA C++:2023 and the C++20 profile on traced host and Cortex-M builds, at level high (see Quality gates ) Docs Strict site build ( _config/mkdocs.yml ), figure and generated-region drift, Doxygen ( _config/Doxyfile ), offline link check, Lighthouse Repository checks One job: DCO on pull requests, the org standard, Markdown and YAML lint, the Kokeb Labs handbook rules for .kokeb/handbook.yml (by rule ID), template drift (warns only) and cppcheck over the driver sources; a second job runs the handbook's source checks (include guards, bus requirements, raw access) CI gate Passes only if every job above passed: the one required check The ESP32 examples job builds every app in examples/esp32/app_config.yml , for each listed ESP-IDF version and build type, with the repository root as the driver's component, and lints the example sources. The gate needs it too. The workflows call the shared, versioned workflows of kokeb-labs/ci-tools at @v1 .
docs.title: CI workflows

docs.text: The tests prove the driver against a model of the chip written from the datasheet; a bench proves the model. The driver states how far it has been checked as a level, in driver.yml ( hardware.level ) and as the README badge: Level Means H0 Host model only: never run on a chip. Releases say not hardware-verified H1 A defined bench rig ran the example; the rig document and the logs are kept H2 A hardware engineer reviewed the rig and the steps and signed off An MCU example ( Examples ) is the bench test: it logs the temperature twice a second. Warm the chip and watch the value rise. Record the rig and the result in the pull request's bench-status section; the hardware-validation skill says what evidence each level needs and how to write the rig document. tools/check_hardware.py keeps the level, the badge and the evidence in step.
docs.title: On hardware

docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ Symptoms, causes and fixes, cheapest check first. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Texas Instruments SNOSD82D D: Device ID and the revision field: 7.6.11 Device ID Register, p. 32 Self-heating and averaging noise: 8.2.2 Detailed Design Procedure, p. 34 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . EnsureInitialized returns Bus ¶ The port reported a failure: either EnsureInitialized() returned false or a transfer did. Check that your port's EnsureInitialized() returns true on its own (log it). Check the bus pins in your port against the board, and that SDA and SCL have pull-ups. With a logic analyser, check that the first frame (a read of Configuration or Device_ID at the address you passed) appears on the bus and is acknowledged. EnsureInitialized returns DeviceIdMismatch ¶ Device_ID did not read 0x117 in bits 11:0. The chip answered with something else, or nothing answered. Symptom Likely cause Fix Bus on the first transaction No ACK at the address Check ADD0 against the address you passed, the pull-ups and V+ 0x0000 or 0xFFFF from Device_ID SDA stuck, or a different device at the address Scan the bus; check SDA continuity 0x0116 or 0x1116 A TMP116 (the driver does not support it) Check the part number on the package 0x0118 or similar Another part at the address Check the part number on the package A TMP119 reads 0x2117 , which the driver cannot tell from a TMP117 of revision 2 and therefore accepts ( A13 ). EnsureInitialized returns Timeout ¶ EEPROM_Busy did not clear after the power-up load. Check V+ (1.8 V to 5.5 V), that the supply rises cleanly, and that reset_timeout_ms is not shorter than the 1.5 ms the datasheet gives plus your port's delay overhead. EnsureInitialized returns BadReply ¶ A bit that must read 0 read 1, or a register did not read back what was written. That is a noisy bus or a line that is not what it should be: lower the clock, shorten the wires, check the pull-ups, and run with Verify::Device to see whether the line itself is stuck. Reads return NoMeasurement ¶ No conversion has finished since the start: a continuous read within the first cycle after EnsureInitialized() , or a chip in shutdown. Wait GetCycleTimeUs(cycle_time, averaging) and read again. With 64 averaged conversions the first result takes a second or more. Reads return UnexpectedReset ¶ The driver saw evidence of a reset: the setting bits of Configuration changed, EEPROM_Busy was set when no programming was running, or a result of 8000h came after a real one. The usual cause is a brown-out on V+. The driver is uninitialised and has stopped writing; EnsureInitialized() writes the configuration again. If it repeats, check the supply and its decoupling. ReadOneShotMilliC returns Timeout ¶ The conversion took longer than (n + 1) x 17.5 ms for n averaged conversions. Check that your port's DelayUs() really waits: a delay that returns at once makes every timeout far too short. The driver sends shutdown before it returns. SetMode, SetAveraging and the other setters return Busy ¶ A one-shot is pending. Wait for it, or end it with SetMode(Mode::Shutdown) . ProgramPowerOnDefaults returns EepromVerifyFailed ¶ Either the readback after the reset differs from what was written, or the chip could not be locked again. Power-cycle the chip, then read the registers with ReadRegister() and compare. The EEPROM allows 1000 writes; a chip that fails to hold the values after a handful of writes is suspect. Read A5 and A6 for what the datasheet leaves open about the relock. ALERT does not fire ¶ Check the polarity: the default is active low, and the pin needs a pull-up. In therm mode ALERT stays on above the high limit until the result falls below the low limit; in alert mode it follows the flags, which clear when Configuration is read. Use GetLatchedStatus() to see what was set. ReadAlertPin() returns Unsupported unless the port has the hook. The comparison at exactly the limit may differ from your expectation ( A8 ). The temperature reads a few degrees high ¶ Self-heating of the board or the chip: a long cycle with shutdown between conversions heats less. Measure the offset against a reference and set Config::offset_mc ; the chip adds it to every result.

docs.text: Figures ¶ Every figure on this site is drawn by a Python module from facts extracted from the code, so it is rebuilt, not redrawn, when the code changes. CI runs kokeb-docs figures --check and fails when a committed figure no longer matches the code. Each figure below lists the files it is drawn from. One register read on the I2C bus ¶ One register read on the I2C bus Figure description and sources Two participants, the host and the TMP117. The host sends START, address 0x48 with the write bit and the pointer byte 0x00, Temp_Result. It repeats START with address 0x48 and the read bit. The chip returns the high byte and the low byte of the register. The host answers the last byte with NACK and ends the transaction with STOP. Drawn from: docs/model/bus-frame.seq.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/bus-frame.seq.yml Drawn from: docs/model/bus-frame.seq.yml I2C timing of the address byte ¶ I2C timing of the address byte Figure description and sources The two lanes are SCL and SDA, left to right in time. SDA falls while SCL is high (the start), the address bits follow, each stable while SCL is high, then the TMP117 pulls SDA low for the acknowledge. The table under the lanes gives each interval with its datasheet value. Drawn from: docs/model/bus-timing.timing.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/bus-timing.timing.yml Drawn from: docs/model/bus-timing.timing.yml Up to four TMP117 on one I2C bus ¶ Up to four TMP117 on one I2C bus Figure description and sources The MCU on top and the TMP117 devices under it connect to the rails SDA and SCL on the right; the dashed card stands for the devices in between. One pull-up per line ties the bus to the supply. Drawn from: docs/model/bus-topology.topology.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/bus-topology.topology.yml Drawn from: docs/model/bus-topology.topology.yml Inside the TMP117 ¶ Inside the TMP117 Figure description and sources The TMP117's function blocks inside its outline. Arrows between blocks carry signals or data in the direction they point (both ways where they have two heads). The package pins stand on the left and right edges with their numbers, each wired to the block it reaches. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . Hardware description: docs/hardware.yml Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml inc/tmp117.hpp inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp What the TMP117 does ¶ What the TMP117 does Figure description and sources Each card is one function of the TMP117: an icon, its name and what it does for the application. The filled pill says how this driver covers it (legend below); the outlined pills are the chip registers behind it. The coverage table in the README gives the driver calls and the datasheet section of each card. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . Hardware description: docs/hardware.yml Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml inc/tmp117.hpp inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp TMP117: Typical connections ¶ TMP117: Typical connections Figure description and sources A schematic. The MCU is on the left, each of its pins level with the chip pin it connects to; above each wire is the hook of the driver's port that drives or reads it. Supply pins point up to their supply and decoupling, ground pins down. Pins on the right carry the loads and the pins tied to a supply or ground; a cross marks a pin left open. A dot is a junction; wires that cross without a dot are not connected. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . Hardware description: docs/hardware.yml Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml inc/tmp117.hpp inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp TMP117: I2C register word ¶ TMP117: I2C register word Figure description and sources One I2C register word of the TMP117, 24 bits in a row from the most significant (left, sent first) to the least significant (right). Each row is one kind of frame; each coloured box a field, with its first and last bit number under it. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . Hardware description: docs/hardware.yml Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml inc/tmp117.hpp inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp TMP117 ¶ TMP117 Figure description and sources The TMP117 in the middle, drawn as its WSON-6 package. On the left the MCU that runs the driver, joined to it by I2C. To the right, what the chip drives, in the order the power flows. Below it, what the chip reads back. The tiles at the bottom are the headline numbers, each with the datasheet section and page it comes from. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . Hardware description: docs/hardware.yml Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml inc/tmp117.hpp inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp TMP117 package, WSON-6 ¶ TMP117 package, WSON-6 Figure description and sources The TMP117 package seen from the top and, when the height is known, from the side, drawn to scale: 2.0 x 2.0 x 0.8 mm. The arrows carry the datasheet's dimensions, the dot marks pin 1 and the pads are numbered counter-clockwise from it, coloured by the pin's electrical type (legend below). Pads sit centred on each side at the stated pitch; the datasheet's land pattern is the reference for a board. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . Hardware description: docs/hardware.yml Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml inc/tmp117.hpp inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp TMP117 pinout, WSON-6 ¶ TMP117 pinout, WSON-6 Figure description and sources The TMP117 seen from the top, in its WSON-6 package. Pin 1 is marked by the dot; the numbers run counter-clockwise from it. Each pad is coloured by the pin's electrical type (legend below). Next to it is the pin's name and, in mono, the hook of the driver's port that drives or reads it; a pin without a hook is not used by the driver. The dashed square is the exposed pad. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . Hardware description: docs/hardware.yml Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml inc/tmp117.hpp inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp Wiring: Typical connections ¶ Wiring: Typical connections Figure description and sources The MCU on the left, the TMP117 in the middle. Each wire to the chip is coloured by the chip pin's electrical type and carries the net name and the chip pin number above it and, under it, the driver hooks that use it (and any part on the net). The boxes underneath list the supplies, the support parts and the pins this circuit leaves unconnected. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/tmp117.hpp ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp . Hardware description: docs/hardware.yml Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml inc/tmp117.hpp inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp The layers, one of them yours ¶ The layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your application calls one object, whose public calls are listed from the umbrella header in inc/. The core turns each call into register reads and writes and hands them to the port contract (the CRTP base in inc/*_interface.hpp), which forwards them, at compile time, to the hooks of the port class you write; your port moves the bytes on the bus. The notes on the right say which layers stay the same on every MCU and which one you write. A library without a port contract has only the first two layers. Drawn from: inc/tmp117.hpp public calls ; inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp I2cInterface ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py Drawn from: public calls in inc/tmp117.hpp I2cInterface in inc/tmp117_i2c_interface.hpp One call through the layers ¶ One call through the layers Figure description and sources Three participants: your code, the core class TMP117 and your port. Your code calls ReadTemperatureMilliC. The core asks the port to write the pointer and read two bytes. A result of 8000h before any conversion ends the call with NoMeasurement, and after one it is evidence of a reset. Otherwise the core multiplies the counts by 7.8125 and returns a Result holding the value 23456 and the status Ok to your code. Drawn from: docs/model/read-call.seq.yml .
